updates.topic: AHA/ASA 2026 acute ischaemic stroke guideline — existence and exact pagination VERIFIED
updates.whatIsNew: CONFIRMED REAL. Published online 26 Jan 2026, print issue August 2026. Crossref, Europe PMC and PubMed (PMID 41582814) all return Stroke, volume 57, issue 8, pages e316-e436, DOI 10.1161/STR.0000000000000513. 65 authors, chair Shyam Prabhakaran; co-vice-chairs Nestor R. Gonzalez and Kori S. Zachrison. It retires the 2018 guideline and its 2019 update. Guideline is built in modular 'knowledge chunk' format; first-ever AHA/ASA recommendations for paediatric AIS; endorses mobile stroke units; tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg within 4.5 h = COR 1. Verified DAPT block (read from the full guideline PDF, section 4.8): Rec 12 = COR 1, LOE A — minor (NIHSS ≤3) non-cardioembolic AIS or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥4) not given IVT: aspirin + clopidogrel (with clopidogrel loading dose 300 or 600 mg) started within 24 h and continued 21 days, then single antiplatelet. Rec 13 = COR 2b, LOE B-R — NIHSS ≤5 or ABCD2 ≥6 or symptomatic ≥50% intra-/extracranial stenosis: ticagrelor + aspirin for 30 days may be considered. Rec 14 = COR 2a, LOE B-R — INSPIRES window, NIHSS ≤5 or high-risk TIA presenting 24–72 h (or NIHSS 4–5 within 24 h) with presumed atherosclerotic cause: clopidogrel + aspirin 21 days then SAPT. Rec 15 = COR 2b, LOE B-R — CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers: ticagrelor + aspirin 21 days then ticagrelor monotherapy may be preferred over clopidogrel-based DAPT. Rec 9 = COR 3 (No Benefit), LOE B-R — ticagrelor monotherapy not recommended over aspirin (SOCRATES). Synopsis states DAPT beyond 90 days is not beneficial and increases bleeding. Also verified: early oral anticoagulation in carefully selected (milder severity) AIS with AF = COR 2a, LOE A.
updates.citation: Prabhakaran S, Gonzalez NR, Zachrison KS, Adeoye O, Alexandrov AW, Ansari SA, et al. 2026 guideline for the early management of patients with acute ischemic stroke: a guideline from the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association. Stroke. 2026;57(8):e316-e436. doi:10.1161/STR.0000000000000513

updates.topic: 2026 AHA/ASA guideline — NEW recommendation against emergency carotid endarterectomy within 48 h (section 4.12)
updates.whatIsNew: This is a CHANGE from the 2019 guideline and is NOT in the document. COR 3 (No Benefit), LOE B-NR: in patients with AIS or unstable neurological status (stroke in evolution) caused by high-grade carotid stenosis or occlusion WITHOUT intracranial occlusion, emergent carotid endarterectomy (within 48 h) is not beneficial for functional outcome. Supporting evidence is a new meta-analysis of 3 RCTs plus 68 observational cohorts (n = 232,952): CEA performed within 2 days of symptom onset versus days 3–14 gave higher 30-day stroke (OR 1.57; 95% CI 1.3–1.9) and higher death (OR 5.19; 95% CI 4.1–6.6). The guideline explicitly defers CEA performed between day 2 and 2 weeks to the AHA/ASA secondary prevention guideline. The document (line 510) states only 'can thiệp nên thực hiện sớm, thường trong vòng 14 ngày' and cites refs [18,107,109,112-114]; it gives no lower bound and does not mention the harm signal from very early surgery.

updates.topic: 2026 AHA/ASA guideline — thrombolysis in mild NON-disabling deficits, and the operational 'clearly disabling' definition (Table 4)
updates.whatIsNew: COR 3 (No Benefit), LOE B-R: in eligible adults presenting with mild non-disabling deficits (e.g. isolated sensory syndrome in many cases) within 4.5 h, IVT is NOT recommended, because it has not shown superiority over dual antiplatelet treatment. Table 4 gives an operational test: 'if the observed deficits persist, would the patient still be able to do basic activities of daily living and/or return to work?' — bathing/dressing, ambulating, toileting, hygiene, eating (BATHE mnemonic). Typically clearly disabling: complete hemianopia (NIHSS vision ≥2), severe aphasia (best language ≥2), severe hemi-attention/extinction to >1 modality (≥2), any weakness limiting sustained effort against gravity (motor ≥2). May not be clearly disabling: isolated mild aphasia, isolated facial droop, mild cortical hand weakness, mild hemimotor loss, hemisensory loss, mild hemisensorimotor loss, mild hemiataxia if still ambulatory. The document covers this framework accurately at lines 255 and 375 but does not name the BATHE mnemonic or the NIHSS item-level cut-offs of Table 4, which would sharpen a doctoral text.

updates.topic: 2024 ESC atrial fibrillation guideline — CHA2DS2-VA replaces CHA2DS2-VASc
updates.whatIsNew: NOT cited anywhere in the document, and this is the single clearest content gap. The 2024 ESC/EACTS guideline drops female sex as a scoring criterion, replacing CHA2DS2-VASc with the sex-neutral CHA2DS2-VA score, and organises all management under the AF-CARE pathway (C = comorbidity/risk-factor management, A = avoiding stroke and thromboembolism, R = reducing symptoms by rate and rhythm control, E = evaluation and dynamic reassessment). Anticoagulation thresholds: CHA2DS2-VA = 0, no anticoagulation; CHA2DS2-VA = 1, oral anticoagulation Class IIa; CHA2DS2-VA ≥2, oral anticoagulation Class I, applied identically to men and women. It also recommends against routinely switching DOAC or adding an antiplatelet after a stroke occurring on anticoagulation (Class III). The document uses CHA2DS2-VASc throughout (lines 59, 189, 197, 316, 460, 486) and at line 189 still gives the sex-split thresholds '≥2 (nam) hoặc ≥3 (nữ)', citing ref [18] (the 2021 AHA secondary prevention guideline). Table 3.8 (line 486) is a CHA2DS2-VASc table. For a monograph claiming currency to August 2026 this needs at least a reconciling paragraph.

Eur Heart J. 2024;45(36):3314-3414. doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehae176

updates.topic: ESO guideline on cerebral small vessel disease, part 2: lacunar ischaemic stroke (2024)
updates.whatIsNew: NOT cited (the document cites no Wardlaw guideline; ref 130 is the unrelated 2014 Wardlaw HTA on MRI cost-effectiveness). Directly on-topic: lacunar stroke is about a quarter of all ischaemic strokes and is 'typically neurologically mild', i.e. the same clinical population as this thesis. GRADE-based; the writing group found little direct evidence, mostly low quality. Recommendations: patients with suspected acute lacunar ischaemic stroke should receive intravenous alteplase, antiplatelet drugs, and should NOT have blood pressure lowered, following general AIS guidelines; for secondary prevention, long-term SINGLE antiplatelet therapy (not DAPT), blood-pressure control and lipid lowering per current guidelines; smoking cessation, exercise, healthy lifestyle, avoid obesity. No recommendation could be made for progressive lacunar stroke or for other drugs. The single-antiplatelet stance for long-term lacunar secondary prevention is a point a monograph on minor stroke should engage with explicitly.
updates.citation: Wardlaw JM, Chabriat H, de Leeuw FE, Debette S, Dichgans M, Doubal F, et al. European Stroke Organisation (ESO) guideline on cerebral small vessel disease, part 2, lacunar ischaemic stroke. Eur Stroke J. 2024;9(1):5-68. doi:10.1177/23969873231219416

updates.topic: 2025 update to the ESO guideline on blood pressure management in acute ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage
updates.whatIsNew: NOT cited. Published in the European Stroke Journal's new OUP format (article ID, no page range). Eight clinical questions, GRADE. Concrete recommendations: advises AGAINST routine pre-hospital BP lowering in suspected stroke (moderate-certainty evidence); in patients undergoing reperfusion, maintain BP <185/110 mmHg before the IVT bolus and <180/105 mmHg during and for 24 h after IVT (low-certainty) and/or mechanical thrombectomy (moderate-certainty); recommends AGAINST intensively lowering systolic BP <140 mmHg in the first 24 h after successful thrombectomy (high-certainty evidence — the only high-certainty recommendation in the document); discourages routine vasopressors to raise BP in AIS patients with neurological deterioration not treated with reperfusion (low-certainty); in acute ICH, expert consensus supports early systolic BP reduction to <140 mmHg for small-to-moderate haematomas. Most recommendations are weak and consensus-based. Relevant to the document's acute-phase BP paragraphs (line 533 onward).
updates.citation: Sandset EC, Palaiodimou L, Jahr SH, Ho L, Fischer U, Katsanos AH, et al. 2025 update to European Stroke Organisation (ESO) guideline on blood pressure management in acute ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage. Eur Stroke J. 2026;11(5):aakag004. doi:10.1093/esj/aakag004

updates.topic: Vietnamese Ministry of Health stroke guideline — Quyết định 3312/QĐ-BYT VERIFIED
updates.whatIsNew: CONFIRMED REAL and the document's citation is accurate. Decision 3312/QĐ-BYT was signed 05/11/2024, takes effect on signature, and replaces Quyết định 5331/QĐ-BYT of 23/12/2020; it applies to all healthcare facilities nationwide. It contains a dedicated chapter 'Hướng dẫn chẩn đoán và điều trị đột quỵ nhẹ và cơn thiếu máu não thoáng qua'. Verified content with numbers: minor stroke defined as NIHSS ≤5. Low-risk TIA (ABCD2 <4): aspirin monotherapy 81–325 mg initially then 81–100 mg/day; alternatives clopidogrel 75 mg/day, aspirin 25 mg + dipyridamole 200 mg twice daily, or cilostazol 100 mg twice daily. High-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥4) and minor stroke NIHSS ≤3: DAPT started within 24 h (optimally within 7 days) — aspirin 81–325 mg then 81–100 mg/day PLUS clopidogrel 300–600 mg loading then 75 mg/day for 21–90 days. High-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥5) and minor stroke NIHSS ≤5: aspirin PLUS ticagrelor 180 mg loading, 90 mg at 12 h, then 90 mg twice daily for 30 days. ABCD2 bands: 0–3 low, 4–5 high, 6–7 very high. Imaging: DWI-MRI to separate minor stroke from TIA. Note the ticagrelor trigger (ABCD2 ≥5) differs from the 2026 AHA/ASA threshold (ABCD2 ≥6 or ≥50% stenosis) — a discrepancy worth an explicit sentence in a Vietnamese doctoral monograph.

updates.topic: CREST-2 — citation and results VERIFIED against the primary source
updates.whatIsNew: CONFIRMED REAL and the document's numbers are exactly right. Crossref and Europe PMC (PMID 41269206) both give N Engl J Med, volume 394, issue 3, pages 219-231, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2508800, print date 15 Jan 2026 (online 21 Nov 2025), first author Thomas G. Brott. Two parallel observer-blinded trials, ≥70% ASYMPTOMATIC carotid stenosis, 155 centres in 5 countries. Stenting trial n=1245: 4-year primary outcome 6.0% (95% CI 3.8–8.3) medical therapy alone vs 2.8% (95% CI 1.5–4.3) stenting + medical, P=0.02 for the absolute difference. Endarterectomy trial n=1240: 5.3% (95% CI 3.3–7.4) medical alone vs 3.7% (95% CI 2.1–5.5) CEA + medical, P=0.24 (not significant). Peri-procedural days 0–44: stenting trial 0 strokes/deaths medical vs 7 strokes and 1 death stenting; endarterectomy trial 3 strokes medical vs 9 strokes CEA. Document line 642 (2.8% vs 6.0%; 3.7% vs 5.3%, non-significant) matches the source. Caveat for the monograph: CREST-2 enrolled ASYMPTOMATIC stenosis only, so it does not bear directly on carotid management after TIA or minor stroke — the document should keep that boundary explicit.
updates.citation: Brott TG, Howard G, Lal BK, Voeks JH, Turan TN, Roubin GS, et al. Medical management and revascularization for asymptomatic carotid stenosis. N Engl J Med. 2026;394(3):219-231. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2508800

updates.topic: Factor XI inhibition — OCEANIC-STROKE (asundexian) main results, the single biggest change in this field since the document's evidence base
updates.whatIsNew: First completed phase 3 trial of an oral FXIa inhibitor for secondary prevention after non-cardioembolic stroke/high-risk TIA. N=12,327 (6162 asundexian 50 mg once daily vs 6165 placebo), randomised within 72 h of non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke (NIHSS ≤15) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 6-7), added on top of planned single or dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT planned in 63%). Median follow-up 567 days. Primary outcome ischaemic stroke: 6.2% vs 8.4%, cause-specific HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.65-0.84), P<0.001 (~26% RRR, ~2% ARR, NNT ≈50 at 1 year). Composite of CV death, MI or stroke also lower. Primary safety outcome ISTH major bleeding: 1.9% vs 1.7%, cause-specific HR 1.10 (95% CI 0.85-1.44) — no bleeding excess. Adverse events 69.3% vs 70.1%; serious AEs 19.2% vs 19.5%. Presented at ISC 2026 (New Orleans), published online 15 April 2026. Note this is exactly the doctoral monograph's target population (TIA/minor-to-moderate stroke, atherothrombotic), so it is not optional background.
updates.citation: Sharma M, Dong Q, Hirano T, Kasner SE, Saver JL, Masjuan J, et al. Asundexian for secondary stroke prevention. N Engl J Med. 2026;394(15):1467-79. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2513880.

updates.topic: Timing of DAPT initiation — large registry analysis directly challenging the document's 24-72 h window claim
updates.whatIsNew: Secondary analysis of the CRCS-K-NIH prospective multicentre registry (20 Korean stroke centres, 2011-2023). N=41,530 with minor non-cardioembolic stroke (NIHSS ≤5) or high-risk TIA presenting within 7 days; 25,112 (60.5%) received DAPT. 90-day composite of recurrent stroke, MI and death: 10.7% (DAPT) vs 11.6% (monotherapy), HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.77-0.87). Benefit was concentrated in initiation within 24 h: HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.69-0.79). NO significant benefit at 24-72 h: HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.88-1.15). Possible HARM beyond 72 h: HR 1.25 (95% CI 1.01-1.55). Time-dependent analysis showed the benefit crossing the null at approximately 42 hours. This is observational and therefore cannot overturn INSPIRES, but the document's statement at line 396/403 that the 24-72 h window is supported should be tempered — the observational signal is that benefit wanes well before 72 h.
updates.citation: Shin J, Lee KJ, Kim CK, Oh K, Kim DY, Kim BJ, et al. Timing of initiation and efficacy of dual antiplatelet therapy in minor stroke or high-risk TIA. Stroke. 2026;57(3):673-83. doi:10.1161/STROKEAHA.125.053343.

updates.topic: CHANCE-3 colchicine — prespecified analysis showing a possible HARM signal in symptomatic intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis
updates.whatIsNew: Prespecified subgroup analysis of CHANCE-3 (244 Chinese centres), n=7567 with baseline intracranial artery assessment. In patients WITH symptomatic intracranial artery stenosis (sICAS), 90-day recurrent stroke was 141/1343 (10.5%) on colchicine vs 115/1352 (8.5%) on placebo, adjusted HR 1.30 (95% CI 1.01-1.69; p=0.04). In patients WITHOUT sICAS: 4.2% vs 5.2%, adjusted HR 0.80 (95% CI 0.62-1.05; p=0.10). Adjusted interaction p=0.01; interaction also significant for the combined vascular event outcome (adjusted p=0.02) and more apparent in elderly patients. The document (line 649) currently reports CHANCE-3 only as a flat neutral trial; this prespecified analysis is a substantively different and clinically important message for a monograph, since sICAS is the dominant mechanism in Asian TIA/minor stroke populations including Vietnam.
updates.citation: Li J, Jing J, Meng X, Shi FD, Gu HQ, Jin A, et al. Colchicine for preventing stroke in patients with and without intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis: a prespecified analysis of a randomized clinical trial. EClinicalMedicine. 2025;84:103226. doi:10.1016/j.eclinm.2025.103226.

updates.topic: CONVINCE — the other pivotal colchicine trial in non-cardioembolic stroke/high-risk TIA, entirely absent from the document
updates.whatIsNew: International randomised open-label blinded-endpoint trial, colchicine 0.5 mg/day plus guideline usual care vs usual care alone, in non-severe non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA. 3154 randomised (3144 in ITT: 1569 vs 1575), median follow-up ~34 months; trial stopped short of the planned 367 outcomes because of COVID-19 budget constraints. Primary composite (recurrent ischaemic stroke, MI, cardiac arrest, hospitalisation for unstable angina): 153/1569 (9.8%) vs 185/1575 (11.7%); incidence rates 3.32 vs 3.92 per 100 person-years; HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.68-1.05), p=0.12 (prespecified alpha 0.048). CRP was lower with colchicine at 28 days and at 1, 2 and 3 years. The document discusses colchicine only through CHANCE-3 — a doctoral monograph cannot omit CONVINCE, which is the long-term counterpart and gives the opposite direction of effect (underpowered rather than flat).
updates.citation: Kelly P, Lemmens R, Weimar C, Walsh C, Purroy F, Barber M, et al. Long-term colchicine for the prevention of vascular recurrent events in non-cardioembolic stroke (CONVINCE): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2024;404(10448):125-33. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(24)00968-1.

updates.topic: TAPIS — early ticagrelor + aspirin DAPT combined with intravenous thrombolysis (positive trial, overturns the 'no DAPT if thrombolysed' rule for moderate stroke)
updates.whatIsNew: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 60 Chinese hospitals; patients thrombolysed for ischaemic stroke with NIHSS 4-10 randomised 1:1 to oral aspirin plus ticagrelor vs placebo started within 6 h of onset (before, during or after thrombolysis); ticagrelor/placebo days 2-7, open-label aspirin days 2-90. N=1382 (690 vs 692), enrolled April 2024 - Sept 2025. Primary outcome mRS 0-1 at 90 days: 474 (68.7%) vs 429 (62.0%), risk ratio 1.11 (95% CI 1.03-1.20), p=0.0089. Symptomatic ICH within 36 h: 6 (0.9%) vs 5 (0.7%), RR 1.20 (95% CI 0.37-3.93), p=0.76. The document's antiplatelet algorithm (line 403) explicitly excludes thrombolysed patients; this trial is the first positive evidence for early DAPT alongside IVT and must be discussed.
updates.citation: Wang A, Xia X, Tang Y, Zhang F, Han X, Li J, et al. Ticagrelor with aspirin dual antiplatelet therapy combined with intravenous thrombolysis in patients with ischaemic stroke in China (TAPIS): a multicentre, double-blind, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2026;407(10542):1919-28. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(26)00757-9.

updates.topic: EAST trial — early clopidogrel + aspirin within 6 h after thrombolysis in MINOR stroke (neutral, and the direct counterpart to TAPIS)
updates.whatIsNew: Multicentre double-blind randomised trial in China (7 Aug 2022 - 1 Aug 2024) in acute ischaemic stroke with NIHSS 0-5 who received intravenous thrombolysis; randomised to clopidogrel plus aspirin or placebo within 6 h after thrombolysis. 1022 randomised, 995 in the modified ITT population (503 vs 492). Primary endpoint mRS 0-1 at 90 days: 89.7% (451/503) vs 89.6% (441/492); odds ratio 1.00 (95% CI 0.67-1.51), P=0.99 — primary endpoint NOT met. Safety profiles similar. Read together with TAPIS this gives the precise nuance a monograph needs: early DAPT after thrombolysis adds nothing when the deficit is already minor (ceiling effect, 90% excellent outcomes), but helps at NIHSS 4-10.
updates.citation: Chen HS, Cui Y, Li XQ, Wang XH, Jiang CH, Li J, et al. Early antiplatelet treatment for minor stroke following thrombolysis: the EAST trial. Eur Heart J. 2026;47(6):746-56. doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf702.

updates.topic: INSPIRES secondary analysis — efficacy by exact time-to-randomisation window (24 h vs 24-48 h vs 48-72 h)
updates.whatIsNew: Prespecified/exploratory subgroup analysis of all 6100 INSPIRES patients by onset-to-randomisation window. ≤24 h (n=783; 401 vs 382): 90-day new stroke 11.5% vs 13.4%, HR 0.83 (95% CI 0.55-1.25). >24-48 h (n=2552; 1255 vs 1297): 7.6% vs 8.9%, HR 0.85 (95% CI 0.65-1.12). >48-72 h (n=2765; 1394 vs 1371): 5.8% vs 8.2%, HR 0.70 (95% CI 0.53-0.94). P for interaction = 0.38 for efficacy, 0.92 for bleeding. Moderate-to-severe bleeding was numerically higher with DAPT in every window (1.5% vs 0.8%; 0.7% vs 0.3%; 0.9% vs 0.4%). The document cites INSPIRES only as a single top-line result; the window-specific data are what actually justify (or qualify) the 24-72 h recommendation it repeats three times.
updates.citation: Liu Y, Zhao J, Gao Y, Chen W, Johnston SC, Bath PM, et al. Clopidogrel and aspirin initiated between 24 to 72 hours for mild ischemic stroke: a subgroup analysis of the INSPIRES randomized clinical trial. JAMA Netw Open. 2024;7(9):e2431938. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.31938.

updates.topic: INSPIRES secondary analysis — time-course of benefit vs risk within the 90 days (the evidence base for the '21 days' rule at the 24-72 h window)
updates.whatIsNew: Post hoc analysis of INSPIRES quantifying when the benefit accrues. Compared with aspirin alone, the reduction in major ischaemic events with clopidogrel-aspirin occurred mainly in the first week (absolute risk reduction 1.42%, 95% CI 0.53%-2.32%), persisted in the second week (ARR 0.49%, 95% CI 0.09%-0.90%) and was no longer significant in the third week (ARR 0.29%, 95% CI -0.05% to 0.62%). This is the direct analogue for INSPIRES of the CHANCE/POINT pooled time-course analysis the document already cites as reference 78, and it strengthens (with real numbers) the claim at line 396 that benefit is front-loaded.
updates.citation: Guan L, Han S, Johnston SC, Bath PM, Amarenco P, Yang Y, et al. Duration of benefit and risk of dual antiplatelet therapy up to 72 hours after mild ischemic stroke and transient ischemic attack. Neurology. 2024;103(7):e209845. doi:10.1212/WNL.0000000000209845.

updates.topic: INSPIRES secondary analysis — treatment effect stratified by baseline recurrence risk (Essen Stroke Risk Score)
updates.whatIsNew: Post hoc analysis of all 6100 INSPIRES patients (median age 65, IQR 57-71; 64.2% male) stratified by Essen Stroke Risk Score and modified ESRS. Clopidogrel-aspirin reduced 90-day new stroke preferentially in patients with LOWER risk-profile scores; the interaction was p=0.07 for ESRS and p=0.01 for modified ESRS. The bleeding hazard did not differ across risk strata (p for interaction 0.21 and 0.85). Counter-intuitive and worth discussion in a monograph section on individualising DAPT, because it argues against simply escalating DAPT in the highest-risk patients.
updates.citation: Zhang Y, Wang X, Gao Y, Chen W, Johnston SC, Amarenco P, et al. Dual antiplatelet treatment up to 72 hours after ischemic stroke stratified by risk profile: a post hoc analysis. Stroke. 2025;56(1):46-55. doi:10.1161/STROKEAHA.124.049246.

updates.topic: CHANCE-2 one-year outcomes — durability of CYP2C19-guided ticagrelor beyond 90 days
updates.whatIsNew: One-year follow-up of the CHANCE-2 randomised trial (6412 CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers with minor stroke or TIA at 202 Chinese centres). New stroke by 1 year: 252 (7.91%) with ticagrelor-aspirin vs 310 (9.73%) with clopidogrel-aspirin, HR 0.80 (95% CI 0.68-0.95), p=0.007. Events occurring between 3 months and 1 year were 61 (2.07%) vs 67 (2.32%) — i.e. essentially the entire benefit was accrued in the first 90 days and then maintained without further divergence. Severe or moderate bleeding at 1 year: 17 (0.53%) vs 20 (0.63%), p=0.61. The document devotes considerable space to CHANCE-2 and to CYP2C19 (13 mentions) but cites only the 2021 primary NEJM paper (ref 16) and the design paper (ref 83); the 1-year data are the correct citation for any claim about durability.
updates.citation: Meng X, Wang A, Tian X, Johnston SC, Li H, Bath PM, et al. One-year outcomes of early therapy with ticagrelor vs clopidogrel in CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers with stroke or TIA trial. Neurology. 2024;102(3):e207809. doi:10.1212/WNL.0000000000207809.

updates.topic: Network meta-analysis of DAPT duration in acute minor non-cardioembolic stroke — quantitative support for the document's '21 days' recommendation
updates.whatIsNew: Systematic review and network meta-analysis, 7 RCTs, 34,646 participants. Versus aspirin alone (efficacy OR for recurrent stroke / bleeding OR): aspirin-clopidogrel 21 days OR 0.75 (95% CI 0.66-0.85) / OR 1.48 (95% CI 1.16-1.89); aspirin-ticagrelor 30 days OR 0.81 (95% CI 0.70-0.95) / OR 3.98 (95% CI 1.74-9.10); aspirin-clopidogrel 90 days OR 0.75 (95% CI 0.60-0.93) / OR 2.02 (95% CI 1.42-2.88). Versus aspirin-clopidogrel 21 days, aspirin-ticagrelor 21 days was more efficacious OR 0.78 (95% CI 0.65-0.92) but with more bleeding OR 1.86 (95% CI 1.39-2.49). Ranking: aspirin-clopidogrel 21 days had the best risk-benefit profile. This is the best available quantitative citation for the document's core claim that 21 days is the right duration and that 90 days buys no extra efficacy while doubling bleeding.
updates.citation: Liu W, Luo S, Huang R, Li Y, Li D, Deng Y. Comparative efficacy and safety of different durations of dual antiplatelet therapy in acute minor non-cardioembolic stroke: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. J Neurol. 2025;272(7):474. doi:10.1007/s00415-025-13210-0.

updates.topic: CONVINCE secondary analyses — colchicine effect by stroke subtype and by presence of atherosclerosis
updates.whatIsNew: (a) Prespecified subtype analysis, n=3100: no interaction across TOAST subtype (p=0.64). Large-artery atherosclerosis 32/260 (12.3%) vs 42/263 (16.0%), HR 0.77 (95% CI 0.48-1.22); small-vessel occlusion 39/419 (9.3%) vs 47/435 (10.8%), HR 0.87 (95% CI 0.57-1.34); cryptogenic 82/877 (9.4%) vs 92/846 (10.5%), HR 0.89 (95% CI 0.66-1.12). (b) Post hoc analysis by presence of atherosclerosis (n=3144, 338 MACE, median 33.6 months): atherosclerosis subgroup 105 (11.1%) vs 132 (14.2%), HR 0.83 (95% CI 0.64-1.07); non-atherosclerosis HR 0.94 (95% CI 0.64-1.39), p interaction 0.60. In the prespecified ON-TREATMENT analysis colchicine reduced MACE in the atherosclerosis subgroup, HR 0.76 (95% CI 0.58-0.99), but not without, HR 0.95 (95% CI 0.63-1.42). Directly supports the document's line-649 thesis that mechanism-based selection is the way forward.
updates.citation: Maes L, Walsh C, Weimar C, Purroy F, Price C, Clarke B, et al. Effect of colchicine for secondary prevention according to stroke subtype: a secondary analysis of the CONVINCE randomized trial. Int J Stroke. 2026;21(7):1009-18. doi:10.1177/17474930251406818. AND McCabe JJ, Lemmens R, Purroy F, Walsh C, Weimar C, Czlonkowska A, et al. Colchicine for secondary prevention after stroke according to the presence of atherosclerosis. Stroke. 2026. Epub 2026 Aug. doi:10.1161/STROKEAHA.126.056561 (volume/pages not yet assigned as of 29 Aug 2026).

updates.topic: Pooled long-term colchicine evidence across vascular beds
updates.whatIsNew: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 6 RCTs with >=12 months' follow-up, 21,800 patients (colchicine 10,871; placebo 10,929), follow-up 12-34 months. Colchicine reduced MACE (CV mortality, MI, ischaemic stroke, urgent coronary revascularisation): pooled HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.56-0.93), driven by reductions in MI, ischaemic stroke and revascularisation. No excess non-cardiovascular death (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.76-1.54). Provides the counterweight to the document's flat 'CHANCE-3 was neutral' framing: the neutrality is duration- and population-specific, not a class verdict.
updates.citation: Samuel M, Berry C, Dubé MP, Koenig W, López-Sendón J, Maggioni AP, et al. Long-term trials of colchicine for secondary prevention of vascular events: a meta-analysis. Eur Heart J. 2025;46(26):2552-63. doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf174.

updates.topic: TACTIS — ticagrelor+aspirin vs cilostazol+aspirin in large-vessel minor stroke/TIA, a cost-relevant comparison for low- and middle-income settings
updates.whatIsNew: Randomised multicentre trial, 900 first-ever large-vessel minor ischaemic stroke or TIA patients randomised 1:1 within 24 h to cilostazol (200 mg load then 100 mg bd to day 90) or ticagrelor (180 mg load then 90 mg bd days 2-90), both plus open-label aspirin (300 mg load then 75 mg od); 857 completed 3-month follow-up. New stroke: 34 (7.6%) cilostazol vs 29 (6.4%) ticagrelor, HR 1.37 (95% CI 0.84-2.26), p=0.21. Composite of new stroke, MI or vascular death: 44 (9.8%) vs 40 (8.9%), HR 1.11 (95% CI 0.64-1.93), p=0.30. Drug-related haemorrhagic complications: 15 (3.3%) vs 30 (6.7%), HR 0.32 (95% CI 0.19-0.68), p=0.01 — significantly FEWER with cilostazol. The document mentions cilostazol only in passing at line 402 as having 'favourable data in Asian populations'; this is the first head-to-head RCT and is directly relevant to a Vietnamese monograph where ticagrelor cost is a real constraint. Note the trial is open to methodological criticism (single-country, no placebo, wide CIs) and should be presented as hypothesis-generating.
updates.citation: Ismaiel M, Ahmed SR, Khalil MFE, Elmesallami AG, Ebied AAMK, Akl AZO, et al. Ticagrelor plus aspirin versus cilostazol plus aspirin in the acute-phase treatment of large-vessel minor stroke or TIA: a randomized controlled multi-center trial, the TACTIS trial. Int J Stroke. 2026;21(7):1019-29. doi:10.1177/17474930251406865.

updates.topic: 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischaemic stroke guideline — the specific antiplatelet recommendation numbers and classes the document paraphrases
updates.whatIsNew: The document already cites this guideline (ref 5) and its paraphrases at lines 396/400/403 are ACCURATE, but it never gives the recommendation numbers or Class/LOE. For a doctoral monograph these should be stated explicitly: 4.8.12 aspirin+clopidogrel within 24 h for NIHSS <=3 or ABCD2 >=4, 21 days then single agent (Class 1, LOE A); 4.8.13 ticagrelor+aspirin 30 days for NIHSS <=5 or ABCD2 >=6 or >=50% stenosis, <24 h (Class 2b, LOE B-R); 4.8.14 DAPT 21 days for NIHSS <=5 or ABCD2 >=4 presenting 24-72 h with presumed atherosclerotic cause >=50% stenosis (Class 2a, LOE B-R); 4.8.15 for CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers, ticagrelor+aspirin for 21 DAYS followed by ticagrelor monotherapy may be reasonable over clopidogrel (Class 2b, LOE B-R) — note this is 21 days, not the 30 days the document implies at line 400; 4.8.9 ticagrelor monotherapy is NOT recommended over aspirin (Class 3 No Benefit, B-R); 4.8.3 IV tirofiban efficacy not well established (Class 2b, B-R); 4.8.10 triple antiplatelet therapy Class 3 Harm. Citation verified: Stroke 2026;57(8):e316-e436, PMID 41582814, online 26 Jan 2026.
updates.citation: Prabhakaran S, Gonzalez NR, Zachrison KS, Adeoye O, Alexandrov AW, Ansari SA, et al. 2026 guideline for the early management of patients with acute ischemic stroke: a guideline from the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association. Stroke. 2026;57(8):e316-e436. doi:10.1161/STR.0000000000000513.

updates.topic: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibition — two new randomised trials of intravenous tirofiban after thrombolysis
updates.whatIsNew: (a) ASSET-IT: phase 3, 38 Chinese centres, non-cardioembolic stroke within 4.5 h not eligible for thrombectomy, 24-h tirofiban infusion started within 60 min after IVT. N=832 (414 tirofiban, 418 placebo); thrombolytic was alteplase 75%, tenecteplase 25%. mRS 0-1 at 90 days 65.9% vs 54.9%, risk ratio 1.20 (95% CI 1.07-1.34), P=0.001; symptomatic ICH 1.7% vs 0%; 90-day mortality 4.1% vs 3.8%. (b) INSTANT: 37 Chinese hospitals, no large/medium vessel occlusion and no cardioembolic source, INADEQUATE clinical response 4-24 h after tenecteplase; n=359 (177 tirofiban, 182 placebo); mRS 0-1 at 90 days 113 (63.8%) vs 95 (52.2%). The document does not mention tirofiban or GP IIb/IIIa at all (0 hits); a monograph covering minor/non-disabling stroke should at minimum note this line of work and the guideline's Class 2b verdict.
updates.citation: Tao C, Liu T, Cui T, Liu J, Li Z, Ren Y, et al. Early tirofiban infusion after intravenous thrombolysis for stroke. N Engl J Med. 2025;393(12):1191-201. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2503678. AND INSTANT Trial Authors for the INSTANT Investigators, Liu X, Zhang F, Zhang C, Li Z, Yuan G, et al. Intravenous tirofiban after tenecteplase in acute ischemic stroke: the INSTANT randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2026;335(22):1949-58. doi:10.1001/jama.2026.5245.

updates.topic: DAPT in stroke/TIA WITHOUT stenotic large-artery atherosclerosis — meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis casting doubt on generalisability
updates.whatIsNew: Systematic review to Nov 2025, 8 publications, of short-term (<=90 days) DAPT vs single antiplatelet in TIA/ischaemic stroke patients with <50% stenosis on vessel imaging. New stroke: RR 0.80 (95% CI 0.65-0.98, p=0.04, I2 25.5%). BUT trial sequential analysis showed a substantial risk of type I error, and a sensitivity analysis restricted to studies including only high-risk TIA or mild ischaemic stroke found NO significant benefit. Moderate-to-severe bleeding increased: OR 2.70 (95% Bayesian CrI 1.28-4.85). No difference in function or mortality. Directly relevant to the document's blanket algorithm at line 403, which applies DAPT on NIHSS/ABCD2 criteria without requiring a demonstrated atherosclerotic substrate.
updates.citation: Ibiapino MK, Ibrahim M, Kumar V, Mamani-Sucari DL, Mantovani SZ, Haitovich I, et al. Dual antiplatelet therapy in stroke without stenotic atherosclerosis: a meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis. Int J Stroke. 2026. Epub 2026 Jul 27. doi:10.1177/17474930261475466 (volume/pages not yet assigned as of 29 Aug 2026; article number 17474930261475466).

updates.topic: Aspirin dose within DAPT — POINT post hoc analysis
updates.whatIsNew: Post hoc analysis of the 2280 POINT patients treated with aspirin plus clopidogrel for 90 days, dichotomised by site-chosen aspirin dose <=100 mg/day (n=1721) vs >100 mg/day (n=559). Composite of ischaemic stroke, MI or ischaemic vascular death: 73/1721 vs 37/559 (p=0.03); adjusted HR for >100 mg 1.62 (95% CI 1.08-2.42). Ischaemic stroke: adjusted HR 1.72 (95% CI 1.13-2.60). No difference in symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (0.7% vs 0.5%, p=0.914). Observational within-trial and confounded by indication (the higher-dose group had more hypertension, heart failure and prior aspirin use), but the document's algorithm at line 403 specifies an aspirin loading dose of 160-325 mg and this analysis is the only direct evidence on maintenance dose within DAPT — worth a cautious sentence favouring low-dose maintenance.
updates.citation: Qureshi AI, Huang Y, Ranjini NJ, Zahoor K, Suri MFK, French BR, et al. The effect of dose of aspirin in high-risk TIA and minor ischemic stroke patients receiving dual antiplatelet medication. J Stroke Cerebrovasc Dis. 2026;35(7):108664. doi:10.1016/j.jstrokecerebrovasdis.2026.108664.

updates.topic: CYP2C19-guided therapy — CHANCE-2 biomarker and comorbidity post hoc analyses
updates.whatIsNew: (a) Lp-PLA2: 5919 CHANCE-2 patients with baseline Lp-PLA2 activity, stratified at the median 188.4 nmol/min/mL. Low Lp-PLA2: ticagrelor-aspirin 5.4% vs clopidogrel-aspirin 7.4%, adjusted HR 0.72 (95% CI 0.54-0.97). High Lp-PLA2: 6.9% vs 8.2%, adjusted HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.65-1.09). Interaction p=0.45 — Lp-PLA2 does NOT modify the effect, a useful negative result. (b) Metabolic syndrome: among 5652 patients (3305 non-MetS, 2347 MetS), ticagrelor-aspirin reduced 90-day recurrence in MetS 6.44% vs 9.90%, HR 0.64 (95% CI 0.48-0.85), with less benefit in non-MetS. Useful for a monograph chapter on refining pharmacogenomic selection beyond genotype alone.
updates.citation: Lin J, Zhou H, Wang Y, Jin A, Li S, Zhang L, et al. Lp-PLA2 activity and genotype-guided dual antiplatelet therapy in minor stroke or transient ischemic attack. Stroke. 2026;57(4):890-6. doi:10.1161/STROKEAHA.125.052954. AND Feng Z, Zhang F, Jin A, Li X, Li Y, Chu Q, et al. Genotype-guided dual antiplatelet therapy in minor stroke or transient ischemic attack with metabolic syndrome: a post hoc analysis of CHANCE-2. Diabetes Obes Metab. 2026;28(1):625-33. doi:10.1111/dom.70243.

updates.topic: Factor XI inhibitor class context — AZALEA-TIMI 71 (abelacimab) and pooled asundexian evidence
updates.whatIsNew: (a) AZALEA-TIMI 71: phase 2b, 1287 AF patients randomised 1:1:1 to abelacimab 150 mg or 90 mg monthly subcutaneously vs open-label rivaroxaban 20 mg; stopped early for a greater-than-expected bleeding reduction. Major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding 3.2 and 2.6 per 100 person-years vs 8.4 with rivaroxaban; HR 0.38 (95% CI 0.24-0.60) and 0.31 (95% CI 0.19-0.51). Free factor XI reduced by 99% (150 mg). (b) Pooled asundexian 50 mg for stroke prevention: 3 RCTs, 14,031 patients; ischaemic stroke RR 0.74 (95% CI 0.63-0.88, p=0.01, I2=0%); any stroke RR 0.75 (95% CI 0.62-0.90, p=0.02); all-cause mortality RR 1.14 (95% CI 0.56-2.32, p=0.50). AZALEA is an AF/anticoagulation trial, not TIA/minor stroke, so it belongs in a class-background paragraph only. The document has zero coverage of factor XI inhibition (0 hits for abelacimab, milvexian, asundexian, 'yếu tố XI') — this is the largest single thematic gap.
updates.citation: Ruff CT, Patel SM, Giugliano RP, Morrow DA, Hug B, Kuder JF, et al. Abelacimab versus rivaroxaban in patients with atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2025;392(4):361-71. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2406674. AND Abbas OF, Amin R, Ghozy S, Hamouda AM, Haddad R, Saha R, et al. Asundexian 50 mg for stroke prevention: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 14,031 patients. Naunyn Schmiedebergs Arch Pharmacol. 2026. Epub 2026 Aug. doi:10.1007/s00210-026-05796-7 (volume/pages not yet assigned as of 29 Aug 2026).

updates.topic: OCEANIC-STROKE supporting documents — design/baseline paper and NEJM editorial
updates.whatIsNew: Design and baseline paper: 12,327 randomised January 2023 - February 2025; 67% male, mean age 68 (SD 11); ischaemic stroke was the index event in 95%, of whom 27.4% had thrombolysis and/or thrombectomy; TOAST distribution 43% large-artery atherosclerosis, 22% small-vessel disease, 30% undetermined, 2% cardioembolic; dual antiplatelets planned in 63%. Entry required NIHSS <=15 or high-risk TIA with ABCD2 6-7, plus at least one of extracranial/intracranial atherosclerosis, history of atherosclerosis, or an imaged acute non-lacunar infarct. Accompanied by an NEJM editorial. These matter for a monograph because the eligibility criteria define exactly which TIA/minor-stroke patients the asundexian result generalises to.

Rationale, design and baseline characteristics of participants in the OCEANIC-STROKE trial of FXIa inhibition for secondary stroke prevention. Eur Stroke J. 2026. updates.topic: ARTESiA subgroup — apixaban vs aspirin in subclinical AF with prior stroke/TIA

updates.topic: CATALYST individual-participant-data meta-analysis — timing of DOAC after AF-related ischaemic stroke
updates.whatIsNew: CONFIRMED EXACTLY AS CITED. One-stage IPD meta-analysis of 4 trials (TIMING NCT02961348, ELAN NCT03148457, OPTIMAS NCT03759938, START NCT03021928); 5441 participants included, primary-outcome data for 5429; mean age 77.7 (SD 10.0), 2472 (45.4%) women, median NIHSS 5 (IQR 3-10). Primary composite (recurrent ischaemic stroke, symptomatic ICH or unclassified stroke within 30 days): 57/2683 (2.1%) early (<=4 days) vs 83/2746 (3.0%) later (>=5 days), OR 0.70 (95% CI 0.50-0.98), p=0.039. Recurrent ischaemic stroke 45 (1.7%) vs 70 (2.6%), OR 0.66 (0.45-0.96), p=0.029. Symptomatic ICH 10 (0.4%) vs 10 (0.4%), OR 1.02 (0.43-2.46), p=0.96. PROSPERO CRD42024522634. The document's volume/issue/pages/DOI, N=5441, 2.1% vs 3.0%, OR 0.70 and the 0.4%/0.4% sICH figures are all correct; only the 95% CI (0.50-0.98) and p values are missing from the text.
updates.citation: Dehbi HM, Fischer U, Åsberg S, Milling TJ, Abend S, Ahmed N, et al. Collaboration on the optimal timing of anticoagulation after ischaemic stroke and atrial fibrillation: a systematic review and prospective individual participant data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (CATALYST). Lancet. 2025;406(10498):43-51. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(25)00439-8. PMID: 40570866.

updates.topic: OPTIMAS full results — early vs delayed DOAC after AF stroke

Primary composite (ischaemic stroke, symptomatic ICH, systemic embolism, unclassified stroke at 90 days) 59/1814 (3.3%) vs 59/1807 (3.3%); adjusted risk difference 0.000 (95% CI -0.011 to 0.012), non-inferiority margin 2 percentage points, p=0.0003 for non-inferiority. Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 11 (0.6%) vs 12 (0.7%). Lancet. 2024;404(10464):1731-41. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(24)02197-4. PMID: 39491870.

updates.topic: ARTESiA — apixaban vs aspirin in device-detected subclinical AF
updates.whatIsNew: 4012 patients, mean age 76.8 (SD 7.6), randomised to apixaban 5 mg twice daily (2.5 mg when indicated) vs aspirin 81 mg daily; mean follow-up 3.5 (SD 1.8) years. Stroke or systemic embolism: 55 events (0.78%/patient-year) with apixaban vs 86 (1.24%/patient-year) with aspirin, HR 0.63 (95% CI 0.45-0.88), p=0.007. Major bleeding (on-treatment): 1.71%/patient-year vs 0.94%/patient-year, HR 1.80 (95% CI 1.26-2.57), p=0.001. Fatal bleeding 5 vs 8. The document contains NO mention of ARTESiA anywhere, yet its section 2.3.2 recommends implantable monitors to find occult AF without addressing whether the AF so found should be anticoagulated.
updates.citation: Healey JS, Lopes RD, Granger CB, et al. Apixaban for stroke prevention in subclinical atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2024;390(2):107-17. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2310234. PMID: 37952132.

updates.topic: NOAH-AFNET 6 — edoxaban vs placebo in atrial high-rate episodes
updates.whatIsNew: 2536 patients randomised (1270 edoxaban, 1266 placebo), terminated early for safety concerns and informal futility at median follow-up 21 months. Primary efficacy composite of cardiovascular death, stroke or systemic embolism: 83 patients (3.2%/patient-year) vs 101 (4.0%/patient-year), HR 0.81 (95% CI 0.60-1.08), p=0.15. Safety composite of death from any cause or major bleeding: 149 (5.9%/patient-year) vs 114 (4.5%/patient-year), HR 1.31 (95% CI 1.02-1.67), p=0.03. Not mentioned anywhere in the document.
updates.citation: Kirchhof P, et al. Anticoagulation with edoxaban in patients with atrial high-rate episodes. N Engl J Med. 2023;389(13):1167-79. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2303062.

updates.topic: Device-detected AF specifically in patients with prior stroke or TIA — pooled ARTESiA + NOAH-AFNET 6 subgroup
updates.whatIsNew: THE MOST DIRECTLY TIA-RELEVANT NEW EVIDENCE. Meta-analysis of the prior-stroke/TIA strata of the two randomised trials: 599 participants (294 anticoagulation, 305 control). Any stroke recurrence RR 0.47 (95% CI 0.23-0.94), p=0.034, NNT 34. Stroke or systemic embolism RR 0.45 (95% CI 0.22-0.90), p=0.023. Major bleeding RR 2.30 (95% CI 1.06-4.98), p=0.035, NNH 37. No significant difference in ischaemic stroke alone, MI, cardiovascular mortality, haemorrhagic stroke or all-cause mortality. This is the quantitative answer to the question the document's section 2.3.2 raises but never resolves: what to do when an implantable monitor finds brief AF after TIA/minor stroke.
updates.citation: Palaiodimou L, Katsanos AH, Melanis K, Stefanou MI, Romoli M, Papagiannopoulou G, et al. Recurrent stroke in patients with history of stroke/transient ischemic attack and device-detected atrial fibrillation: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur Stroke J. 2025;10(4):1221-30. doi:10.1177/23969873251334278. PMID: 40265470.

updates.topic: Pooled study-level meta-analysis of NOAH-AFNET 6 and ARTESiA
updates.whatIsNew: Study-level meta-analysis of the two device-detected-AF trials establishing the now-standard summary: DOACs reduce ischaemic stroke but increase major bleeding in device-detected AF, with a much smaller absolute stroke benefit than in clinical AF. This is the paper most guideline groups cite when framing the trade-off; useful as the single reference for a monograph paragraph on subclinical AF. (I confirmed the citation metadata via Crossref; I did not retrieve the pooled point estimates, so quote them only after reading the paper.)
updates.citation: McIntyre WF, et al. Direct oral anticoagulants for stroke prevention in patients with device-detected atrial fibrillation. Circulation. 2024;149(13):981-8. doi:10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.123.067512.

updates.topic: Device-detected AF with vs without vascular disease — combined NOAH-AFNET 6 + ARTESiA analysis
updates.whatIsNew: Combined analysis of NOAH-AFNET 6 (n=2534) and ARTESiA (n=4012). Vascular disease present in 56% (NOAH-AFNET 6) and 46% (ARTESiA). With vascular disease, primary composite 3.9 vs 5.0 per 100 patient-years (NOAH-AFNET 6) and 3.2% vs 4.4% (ARTESiA) favouring anticoagulation; major bleeding IRR 1.55 (95% CI 1.10-2.20). Without vascular disease, primary outcome 2.7%/patient-year and 2.3%/patient-year with no difference between arms; major bleeding IRR 1.93 (95% CI 0.72-5.20). Interaction p=0.08. Supports selecting patients with established vascular disease (which includes prior TIA/stroke) for anticoagulation of device-detected AF.
updates.citation: Schnabel RB, et al. Anticoagulation in device-detected atrial fibrillation with or without vascular disease: a combined analysis of the NOAH-AFNET 6 and ARTESiA trials. Eur Heart J. 2024;45(46):4902-16. doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehae596. PMID: 39222018.

updates.topic: CHAMPION-AF — Watchman FLX LAAO vs DOAC in patients ELIGIBLE for anticoagulation
updates.whatIsNew: MAJOR NEW EVIDENCE THAT SUPERSEDES THE DOCUMENT'S LAAO SECTION. 3000 patients randomised (1499 device, 1501 anticoagulation), mean age 71.7 years, mean CHA2DS2-VASc 3.5. Primary efficacy composite (cardiovascular death, stroke or systemic embolism at 3 years): 5.7% (81) device vs 4.8% (65) anticoagulation; difference 0.9 percentage points (95% CI -0.8 to 2.6), p<0.001 for non-inferiority against a 4.8-percentage-point margin. Primary safety endpoint (non-procedure-related bleeding): 10.9% (154) vs 19.0% (260), HR 0.55 (95% CI 0.45-0.67), p<0.001 for superiority. The document's section 3.4.4 rests entirely on PROTECT-AF/PREVAIL 5-year data (2017) and PRAGUE-17 (2020) and states LAAO is only for anticoagulation-ineligible patients — a position this trial directly tests in anticoagulation-ELIGIBLE patients.
updates.citation: Doshi SK, Kar S, Nair DG, et al. Left atrial appendage closure or anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2026;394(21):2083-94. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2517213. PMID: 41910347.

updates.topic: CLOSURE-AF — LAAO vs physician-directed medical therapy in high stroke and bleeding risk AF
updates.whatIsNew: THE NEGATIVE COUNTERWEIGHT TO CHAMPION-AF, and closest to the population the document describes (bleeding-limited patients). 912 patients randomised in Germany (446 device, 442 medical therapy); mean age 77.9 (SD 7.1), 38.6% female, mean CHA2DS2-VASc 5.2 (SD 1.5), mean HAS-BLED 3.0 (SD 0.9); median follow-up 3 years (IQR 1.7-4.7). Primary composite (stroke, systemic embolism, major bleeding, or cardiovascular/unexplained death): 155 events, 16.8 per 100 patient-years with device vs 127 events, 13.3 per 100 patient-years with medical therapy. Difference in restricted mean survival time -0.36 years (95% CI -0.70 to -0.01); LAAO was NOT non-inferior. Serious adverse events 82.5% vs 77.4%.
updates.citation: Landmesser U, et al. Left atrial appendage closure or medical therapy in atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2026;394(13):1270-80. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2513310. PMID: 41849741.

updates.topic: OPTION — LAAO vs oral anticoagulation after AF catheter ablation
updates.whatIsNew: 1600 patients randomised (803 LAAO, 797 anticoagulation), mean age 69.6 (SD 7.7), 34.1% women, mean CHA2DS2-VASc 3.5. Primary efficacy (death from any cause, stroke or systemic embolism at 36 months) 5.3% vs 5.8%, p<0.001 for non-inferiority. Primary safety (non-procedure-related major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding) 8.5% vs 18.1%, p<0.001 for superiority. Major bleeding through 36 months 3.9% vs 5.0%, p<0.001 for non-inferiority. 23 procedure-related complications in the LAAO arm. A 2026 sub-analysis found LAAO did not affect AF recurrence after ablation (49.2% vs 45.5%, p=0.08).
updates.citation: Wazni OM, et al. Left atrial appendage closure after ablation for atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2025;392(13):1277-87. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2408308. PMID: 39555822.

updates.topic: CATALYST left atrial appendage occlusion trial (Amulet vs NOAC) — ONGOING, NO RESULTS
updates.whatIsNew: NO RESULTS EXIST. NCT04226547 (Abbott Medical Devices), 'Amplatzer Amulet LAAO vs. NOAC', acronym CATALYST, enrolment 2650, status active/not recruiting, primary completion date January 2029. Do not cite any efficacy figure for this trial. IMPORTANT FOR THE DOCUMENT: this LAAO trial shares its acronym with the anticoagulation-timing IPD meta-analysis already cited as reference 101. If the monograph ever mentions 'CATALYST' for LAAO it must disambiguate, otherwise a reader will conflate two entirely unrelated studies.

updates.topic: AMALFI — remote mail-based ECG-patch screening for AF in high-risk older people
updates.whatIsNew: 5040 participants randomised 1:1 (2520 per arm), mean age 78 (SD 6), 47% female, CHA2DS2-VASc >=3 (men) or >=4 (women); mail-based ECG-patch screening vs usual care. AF recorded by 2.5 years: 172 (6.8%) vs 136 (5.4%), ratio of proportions 1.26 (95% CI 1.02-1.57), p=0.03. Mean anticoagulation exposure 1.63 months (95% CI 1.50-1.76) vs 1.14 months (1.01-1.26), difference 0.50 months (0.24-0.75), p<0.001. Stroke 69 (2.7%) vs 64 (2.5%), rate ratio 1.08 (95% CI 0.76-1.53) — screening increased detection but did not reduce stroke. Directly relevant to the document's Table 2.4 on detection yields, and a corrective to the implicit assumption that more detection equals fewer strokes.
updates.citation: Wijesurendra RS, et al. Remote screening for asymptomatic atrial fibrillation: the AMALFI randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2025;334(15):1349-57. doi:10.1001/jama.2025.15440. PMID: 40878848.

updates.topic: GUARD-AF — population screening with 14-day ECG patch to prevent stroke
updates.whatIsNew: 11905 participants in the intention-to-treat population, randomised 1:1 to screening vs usual care; median age 75 years, 56.6% female; median follow-up 15.3 months. AF diagnosed in 5.0% (screening) vs 3.3% (usual care); anticoagulation started in 4.2% vs 2.8%. Stroke 0.7% vs 0.6%, HR 1.10 (95% CI 0.69-1.75). Bleeding 1.0% vs 1.1%, HR 0.87 (95% CI 0.60-1.26). Together with AMALFI this establishes that screening-detected AF has not yet been shown to reduce stroke — an essential caveat for any monograph chapter advocating prolonged monitoring.
updates.citation: Lopes RD, et al. Effect of screening for undiagnosed atrial fibrillation on stroke prevention. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2024;84(21):2073-84. doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2024.08.019. PMID: 39230544.

updates.topic: 2024 ESC guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation
updates.whatIsNew: The current European guideline governing anticoagulation, AF definitions and device-detected AF, published August/September 2024 and incorporating the AF-CARE framework. The document cites the 2026 AHA/ASA acute-stroke guideline and the Vietnamese Ministry of Health 2024 decision but no contemporary cardiology AF guideline, which is a conspicuous gap in chapters 2.3 and 3.4 (CHA2DS2-VASc, DOAC dosing, occult AF).
updates.citation: Van Gelder IC, et al. 2024 ESC guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation developed in collaboration with the European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS). Eur Heart J. 2024;45(36):3314-414. doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehae176.

updates.topic: OCEANIC-STROKE — asundexian (factor XIa inhibitor) for secondary prevention after non-cardioembolic stroke or high-risk TIA
updates.whatIsNew: OUTSIDE THE AF QUESTION BUT THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT OMISSION FOR A TIA/MINOR-STROKE MONOGRAPH. 12327 patients randomised (6162 asundexian 50 mg daily, 6165 placebo) on top of antiplatelet therapy, in non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA. Primary efficacy outcome recurrent ischaemic stroke 6.2% vs 8.4%, cause-specific HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.65-0.84), p<0.001. Major bleeding 1.9% vs 1.7%, cause-specific HR 1.10 (95% CI 0.85-1.44). Adverse events 69.3% vs 70.1%. The document's chapter 3 antiplatelet discussion and its 'future directions' passage (line 653, which lists only TEMPO-2 and CHANCE-3 as negative) contains no mention of asundexian or factor XI inhibition at all; a monograph claiming currency to August 2026 cannot omit the first positive phase 3 factor XIa trial in this exact population.
updates.citation: Sharma M, et al. Asundexian for secondary stroke prevention. N Engl J Med. 2026;394(15):1467-79. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2513880. PMID: 41985132.

updates.topic: AI-enabled ECG risk-guided AF screening (VITAL-AF secondary analysis)
updates.whatIsNew: CITATION CONFIRMED, EFFECT SIZES NOT RETRIEVED — cite only after reading the paper. A 2026 JACC analysis of the VITAL-AF randomised screening trial applying AI-enabled ECG models to target screening. This is the closest thing that exists to an AI-ECG AF-screening trial result; I found NO randomised controlled trial in which AI-ECG screening was itself the randomised intervention with clinical outcomes. Related confirmed work: AI-enabled analysis of handheld single-lead ECGs to predict incident AF in VITAL-AF (NPJ Digit Med. 2025;8(1):776. doi:10.1038/s41746-025-02164-2).
updates.citation: Risk-guided atrial fibrillation screening with AI-enabled ECG models: an analysis of the VITAL-AF trial. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2026;87(14):1798-813. doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2026.01.087. PMID: 41983618. (Title as returned by Europe PMC may be abbreviated; verify author list and exact title before citing.)

updates.topic: CREST-2 primary results (both parallel trials)
updates.whatIsNew: CONFIRMED PUBLISHED, and the document's citation is exactly correct. Two parallel observer-blinded RCTs, 155 centres, 5 countries, asymptomatic stenosis >=70%. Stenting trial n=1245; endarterectomy trial n=1240. Primary outcome = any stroke or death to day 44, plus ipsilateral ischaemic stroke thereafter to 4 years. Stenting trial: 4-year incidence 2.8% (95% CI 1.5-4.3) with CAS+IMM vs 6.0% (95% CI 3.8-8.3) with IMM alone, P=0.02 for the absolute difference. Endarterectomy trial: 3.7% (95% CI 2.1-5.5) with CEA+IMM vs 5.3% (95% CI 3.3-7.4) with IMM alone, P=0.24. The document's figures (2.8 vs 6.0; 3.7 vs 5.3, not significant) match the published abstract exactly.
updates.citation: Brott TG, Howard G, Lal BK, Voeks JH, Turan TN, Roubin GS, et al.; CREST-2 Investigators. Medical management and revascularization for asymptomatic carotid stenosis. N Engl J Med. 2026;394(3):219-31. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2508800. PMID: 41269206.

updates.topic: CREST-2 - magnitude and severity of the prevented events (critical appraisal)
updates.whatIsNew: Independent appraisal quantifies what the document argues only qualitatively. Across both trials only 104 primary-outcome infarctions occurred in 2485 patients over 4 years (4.2%), and 70 of them (67%) were minor strokes. Major strokes were essentially equal in every arm: stenting 4 vs IMM1 5; endarterectomy 3 vs IMM2 5. A tipping-point analysis showed that 3 additional primary events in the stenting arm would have abolished statistical significance, and 6 additional events in IMM2 would have made endarterectomy significant. A companion re-analysis using an aggregated control arm reports ARR 2.85% for CAS (NNT 35) and 1.95% for CEA, with the headline results unchanged.
updates.citation: Darsaut TE, Raymond J, Iancu D, Chagnon M, Gevry G, Fahed R. Understanding statistical versus clinical significance: a critical appraisal of the CREST-2 study. Neurochirurgie. 2026;72(3):101798. doi:10.1016/j.neuchi.2026.101798. PMID: 41886913. // Musialek P, et al. CREST-2 findings are unchanged using an aggregated control group for the CAS and CEA trial. Postepy Kardiol Interwencyjnej. 2026;22(2):178-89. doi:10.5114/aic.2026.163187. PMID: 42598485.

updates.topic: ECST-2 (Second European Carotid Surgery Trial) - 2-year interim results
updates.whatIsNew: NOT COVERED AT ALL. The document cites only the original 1998 ECST (ref 108) and uses 'ECST' solely as a stenosis-measurement method (Figure 3.2). ECST-2 is a separate modern RCT in asymptomatic or low-to-intermediate-risk symptomatic carotid stenosis (Carotid Artery Risk score <20%): 429 patients randomised (215 optimised medical therapy alone vs 214 OMT plus revascularisation), median age 72, 69% male. Two-year hierarchical win-ratio analysis of the composite (periprocedural death/fatal stroke/fatal MI, non-fatal stroke, non-fatal MI, new silent cerebral infarct): win ratio 1.01 (95% CI 0.60-1.70), p=0.97 - 5228 wins (11.4%) for OMT alone vs 5173 (11.3%) for OMT plus revascularisation, 77.3% ties. No evidence of benefit from adding revascularisation. This is an interim analysis; recruitment target was substantially larger.
updates.citation: Donners SJA, van Velzen TJ, Cheng SF, Gregson J, Bulbulia R, Halliday A, et al.; ECST-2 Investigators. Optimised medical therapy alone versus optimised medical therapy plus revascularisation for asymptomatic or low-to-intermediate risk symptomatic carotid stenosis (ECST-2): a multicentre, randomised trial. Lancet Neurol. 2025;24(5):389-99. doi:10.1016/S1474-4422(25)00107-3. PMID: 40252662.

updates.topic: Meta-analysis of the three modern asymptomatic-carotid RCTs (CREST-2 + ECST-2 + SPACE-2)
updates.whatIsNew: Directly qualifies the document's CREST-2-only framing. Three RCTs, 3426 patients. Primary composite (stroke or death, or ipsilateral ischaemic stroke): 4.76% (88/1847) with revascularisation vs 6.40% (101/1579) with medical management; RR 0.91 (95% CI 0.47-1.74), P=0.77, with high heterogeneity (I2=74%). All-cause mortality 7.7% vs 9.50%; RR 0.83 (95% CI 0.67-1.04). Subgroups: CEA RR 0.73 (95% CI 0.45-1.19); CAS RR 0.72 (95% CI 0.23-2.27). Conclusion: contemporary medical management carries comparable stroke and mortality risk to revascularisation. A second independent meta-analysis of the same three trials reaches similar conclusions.
updates.citation: Gao Y, Wang L, Zhang H, et al. Medical management and revascularization for asymptomatic carotid stenosis: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. J Neurol. 2026;273(4):220. doi:10.1007/s00415-026-13766-5. PMID: 41860631. // Ali A, Cheema WA, Nisar F, et al. Modern management of asymptomatic carotid stenosis: a meta-analysis of CREST-2, SPACE-2, and ECST-2. Ann Clin Transl Neurol. 2026 Jul 13 [online ahead of print; no volume/pages assigned]. doi:10.1002/acn3.70479. PMID: 42439053.

updates.topic: SPACE-2 - 5-year results (context for the asymptomatic carotid section)
updates.whatIsNew: NOT CITED anywhere in the document. SPACE-2 is the third modern asymptomatic-carotid RCT and one of the three trials pooled in the 2026 meta-analyses. Its 5-year results were published in 2022 (i.e. before the 2024-2026 window), so it is background rather than new evidence, but its absence leaves the document's asymptomatic-carotid section resting on CREST-2 alone. Trial randomised CEA vs CAS vs best medical treatment alone in moderate-to-severe asymptomatic stenosis; enrolment was terminated early for slow recruitment.
updates.citation: Reiff T, Eckstein HH, Mansmann U, Jansen O, Fraedrich G, Mudra H, et al.; SPACE-2 Investigators. Carotid endarterectomy or stenting or best medical treatment alone for moderate-to-severe asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis: 5-year results of a multicentre, randomised controlled trial. Lancet Neurol. 2022;21(10):877-88. doi:10.1016/S1474-4422(22)00290-3. PMID: 36115360.

updates.topic: CASSISS - long-term (median 7.4-year) follow-up
updates.whatIsNew: The document cites only the 2022 JAMA CASSISS report (ref 116). Extended follow-up of all 358 randomised patients (stenting 176 vs medical therapy 182), followed to 22 January 2024, median follow-up 7.4 years (IQR 6.0-8.0). Primary composite (stroke or death within 30 days, or stroke in the qualifying artery territory beyond 30 days): 14.8% stenting vs 14.3% medical, HR 1.02 (95% CI 0.58-1.77), P=0.97. Disabling stroke or death 16.5% vs 14.3%, HR 1.12 (95% CI 0.66-1.91), P=0.70. Death 9.1% vs 7.1%, HR 1.22 (95% CI 0.58-2.58), P=0.60. This is the strongest available long-term evidence for the document's statement that intracranial stenting is not first-line.
updates.citation: Gao P, He X, Wang H, Chen Y, Wang T, Yang R, et al. Stenting versus medical therapy for symptomatic intracranial artery stenosis: long-term follow-up of a randomized trial. Stroke. 2025;56(5):1128-37. doi:10.1161/STROKEAHA.124.049602. PMID: 40099362.

updates.topic: SAMMPRIS + CASSISS preplanned pooled individual-patient-data analysis
updates.whatIsNew: Pools the two trials the document already cites (refs 72 and 116) into one IPD analysis: 809 patients (451 SAMMPRIS, 358 CASSISS); 400 percutaneous transluminal angioplasty and stenting (PTAS) vs 409 medical. Primary outcome (stroke or death within 30 days, or ischaemic stroke in the qualifying territory beyond 30 days) 17.5% vs 13.2%, HR 1.37 (95% CI 0.96-1.95), P=0.08 - not significant. But 30-day stroke or death was clearly higher with PTAS: 10.5% vs 4.2%, HR 2.62 (95% CI 1.49-4.61), P<0.001. Higher PTAS risk in white patients (HR 1.97, 95% CI 1.17-3.31), hyperlipidaemia (HR 2.04, 95% CI 1.27-3.26) and TIA presentation (HR 2.19, 95% CI 1.08-4.45) - the TIA finding is directly on-topic for this monograph.
updates.citation: Wang T, Luo J, Li T, Wang X, Gao P, Yang R, et al. Stenting versus medical treatment alone for symptomatic intracranial artery stenosis: a preplanned pooled individual patient data analysis. J Neurointerv Surg. 2025;17(10):1032-9. doi:10.1136/jnis-2024-022189. PMID: 39147573.

updates.topic: BASIS - submaximal balloon angioplasty for symptomatic intracranial stenosis (first POSITIVE endovascular RCT in sICAS)
updates.whatIsNew: NOT COVERED, and it directly qualifies the document's blanket statement (line 524) that trials 'do not support intracranial stenting'. BASIS tested balloon angioplasty (not stenting) plus aggressive medical management vs aggressive medical management alone in 70-99% symptomatic intracranial stenosis, 31 Chinese centres. 512 randomised, 501 analysed (mean age 58.0 years; 31.5% women; 249 angioplasty vs 252 medical). Primary composite: 4.4% vs 13.5%; HR 0.32 (95% CI 0.16-0.63); P<.001. 30-day any stroke or all-cause death 3.2% vs 1.6%. Beyond 30 days to 1 year: ischaemic stroke in the qualifying territory 0.4% vs 7.5%; revascularisation of the qualifying artery 1.2% vs 8.3%. Symptomatic ICH 1.2% vs 0.4%. Procedural complications 17.4%; arterial dissection 14.5%. Caveats for the monograph: single-country, 1-year outcome, high procedural complication rate, and an unusually high 13.5% event rate in the medical arm.
updates.citation: Sun X, Deng Y, Zhang Y, Yang M, Sun D, Nguyen TN, et al.; BASIS Investigators. Balloon angioplasty vs medical management for intracranial artery stenosis: the BASIS randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2024;332(13):1059-69. doi:10.1001/jama.2024.12829. PMID: 39235816.

updates.topic: Drug-coated balloons for intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis - two randomised trials
updates.whatIsNew: NOT COVERED. Two RCTs now exist, both comparing DCB with bare-metal stenting (not with medical therapy). (1) DR. BEYOND, 14 Chinese tertiary hospitals, 209 participants (103 DCB vs 106 BMS), median age 59: 6-month angiographic restenosis 11% vs 29%, RR 0.38 (95% CI 0.19-0.78), P=.006; 6-month symptomatic restenosis 1% vs 10%, RR 0.13 (95% CI 0.02-0.96), P=.02; 30-day-to-1-year recurrent ischaemic events 4% vs 13%, HR 0.31 (95% CI 0.10-0.94), P=.04; 30-day stroke or death 6% vs 5%, HR 1.24 (95% CI 0.38-4.05), P=.73. (2) AcoArt sICAS, 201 randomised / 180 analysed, mean age 58: 6-month target-lesion restenosis 6.9% vs 32.9%, OR 0.15 (95% CI 0.05-0.42), P=0.0003; 30-day target-vessel stroke or death 4.4% vs 5.6%, OR 0.79 (95% CI 0.21-3.05), P=0.73. Both show DCB reduces restenosis versus BMS with comparable periprocedural safety; neither establishes any device against optimal medical therapy.
updates.citation: Guan S, Tong X, Li X, Wang B, Jia B, Gao F, et al. Drug-coated balloon for endovascular treatment of symptomatic intracranial stenotic disease: a multicenter randomized controlled trial. Radiology. 2026;318(1):e250893. doi:10.1148/radiol.250893. PMID: 41557900. // Ma G, Sun D, Jia B, Ling L, Nguyen TN, Sun X, et al. Comparison of drug-coated balloon with bare-metal stent in patients with symptomatic intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis: the AcoArt sICAS randomized clinical trial. J Neurointerv Surg. 2026;18(2):500-7. doi:10.1136/jnis-2024-022768. PMID: 41815310 (record set).

updates.topic: DISTAL - thrombectomy for medium/distal vessel occlusion
updates.whatIsNew: The document asserts the conclusion (line 376: 'recent trials have not demonstrated routine benefit for medium or distal occlusion') but names NO trial and cites only the guideline [5] and a narrative review [74]. DISTAL: 543 participants randomised (271 EVT plus best medical treatment vs 272 BMT alone), women 44%, median age 77, median admission NIHSS 6 (IQR 5-9) - i.e. a MINOR-STROKE population, squarely on-topic. IV thrombolysis in 65.4%. Occlusions: M2 44.0%, M3 26.9%, P2 13.4%, P1 5.5%. Primary outcome (90-day mRS shift): common OR for improvement 0.90 (95% CI 0.67-1.22), P=0.50. All-cause mortality 15.5% vs 14.0%; symptomatic ICH 5.9% vs 2.6%.
updates.citation: Psychogios M, Brehm A, Ribo M, Rizzo F, Strbian D, Raty S, et al.; DISTAL Investigators. Endovascular treatment for stroke due to occlusion of medium or distal vessels. N Engl J Med. 2025;392(14):1374-84. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2408954. PMID: 39908430.

updates.topic: ESCAPE-MeVO - thrombectomy for medium vessel occlusion
updates.whatIsNew: Also not named or cited. 530 patients from five countries enrolled April 2022-June 2024 (255 EVT vs 275 usual care), presenting within 12 hours with favourable baseline non-invasive imaging; 84.7% had a primary MCA-branch occlusion. Primary outcome mRS 0-1 at 90 days: 106/255 (41.6%) EVT vs 118/274 (43.1%) usual care; adjusted rate ratio 0.95 (95% CI 0.79-1.15), P=0.61. Importantly for a risk-benefit discussion, 90-day mortality was HIGHER with EVT: 13.3% vs 8.4%, adjusted HR 1.82 (95% CI 1.06-3.12); symptomatic ICH 14/257 (5.4%) vs 6/272 (2.2%). Published back-to-back with DISTAL, with an accompanying editorial (Nogueira RG, Rocha M. Medium- and distal-vessel occlusion - the limit of thrombectomy? N Engl J Med. 2025;392(14):1440-2. doi:10.1056/NEJMe2500492).
updates.citation: Goyal M, Ospel JM, Ganesh A, Dowlatshahi D, Volders D, Mohlenbruch MA, et al.; ESCAPE-MeVO Investigators. Endovascular treatment of stroke due to medium-vessel occlusion. N Engl J Med. 2025;392(14):1385-95. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2411668. PMID: 39908448.

updates.topic: DISCOUNT - thrombectomy for medium/distal occlusion (third negative trial, 2026)
updates.whatIsNew: Newest of the three MeVO trials and published after most reviews the document may rely on. 22 French stroke centres, November 2021-April 2025, stopped early at 244 of a planned 488 patients (median age 75 [IQR 67-81]; 56% male; median NIHSS 8 [IQR 6-12]). 100 of 123 assigned to thrombectomy (81%) actually received it; 217 (89%) completed follow-up. Good clinical outcome at 3 months: 72/116 (62%) thrombectomy vs 81/119 (68%) control; OR 0.73 (95% CI 0.40-1.31); P=.29. Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 11% vs 3%, P=.008. Mortality 6% vs 8%, P=.49. NOTE: published online-first on 22 July 2026 - NO volume, issue or page numbers have been assigned yet, so it must be cited as an ahead-of-print item.
updates.citation: Clarencon F, Bala F, Baptiste A, Marnat G, Gory B, Sibon I, et al.; DISCOUNT Investigators. Mechanical thrombectomy in ischemic stroke with a medium or distal arterial occlusion: the DISCOUNT randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2026 Jul 22 [online ahead of print]. doi:10.1001/jama.2026.8977. PMID: 42485024.

updates.topic: 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischaemic stroke guideline - citation confirmed, but a published CORRECTION exists
updates.whatIsNew: CONFIRMED: the document's ref 5 is exactly right (Stroke. 2026;57(8):e316-e436, doi:10.1161/STR.0000000000000513, PMID 41582814). However, an official correction to that guideline was published in the same issue (Stroke. 2026;57(8):e461-e467, doi:10.1161/STR.0000000000000530, PMID 42507797), and a further letter proposing additional corrections appeared the following month (Albers GW, Warach SJ, Saver JL. Proposed corrections to the 2026 guideline for the early management of patients with acute ischemic stroke. Stroke. 2026;57(9):2935-8, doi:10.1161/STROKEAHA.126.056478, PMID 42535283). Stroke. 2026;57(8):e316-e436. doi:10.1161/STR.0000000000000513. Correction: Stroke. 2026;57(8):e461-e467. doi:10.1161/STR.0000000000000530.

updates.topic: Post-CREST-2 interpretive literature for the asymptomatic-carotid section
updates.whatIsNew: Two pieces are worth citing beside CREST-2 itself, both written for exactly the interpretive caution the document already voices in section 3.5.4. Kelly, McCabe and De Borst set out the main results and their reading for practice; Paraskevas et al. compare CREST-2 with ECST-2 side by side. No formal AHA/ASA or ESVS carotid guideline update has yet been issued in response to CREST-2 (see notFound), so these commentaries are currently the closest thing to consensus interpretation.

Semin Vasc Surg. 2026;39(2):180-4. PMID: 42285646.

updates.topic: Expert guidance on acute treatment of disabling vs non-disabling minor ischaemic stroke

Relevant to the document's line 376 discussion of low-NIHSS proximal occlusion and to its framing of TEMPO-2. Not cited in the document.
