updates.topic: Factor XI inhibition after minor stroke/high-risk TIA — OCEANIC-STROKE (asundexian), phase 3, PUBLISHED
updates.whatIsNew: Landmark positive phase 3 trial, entirely absent from the document. 12,327 patients (6,162 asundexian 50 mg once daily vs 6,165 placebo) randomised within 72 h of non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA, on top of planned single or dual antiplatelet therapy. Enrichment required a non-lacunar infarct, a history of atherosclerosis, or atherosclerotic plaque on cerebrovascular imaging. Primary efficacy outcome ischaemic stroke: 6.2% asundexian vs 8.4% placebo, cause-specific HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.65–0.84), P<0.001. Composite of cardiovascular death, MI or stroke also lower. Primary safety outcome major bleeding: 1.9% vs 1.7%, cause-specific HR 1.10 (95% CI 0.85–1.44). Adverse events 69.3% vs 70.1%; serious adverse events 19.2% vs 19.5%. Funded by Bayer; NCT05686070. IMPORTANT CAVEAT for accurate use: this is NOT an ESUS trial — cardioembolic sources were excluded and the population was enriched for atherosclerosis, so it does not resolve the ESUS anticoagulation question; no ESUS-specific subgroup publication exists. Accompanying editorial: Boulanger M. Asundexian for noncardioembolic ischemic stroke. N Engl J Med. 2026;394(15):1540-1. doi:10.1056/NEJMe2601859.
updates.citation: Sharma M, Dong Q, Hirano T, Kasner SE, Saver JL, Masjuan J, et al. Asundexian for secondary stroke prevention. N Engl J Med. 2026;394(15):1467-79. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2513880.

updates.topic: Factor XI inhibition — LIBREXIA-STROKE (milvexian): ONGOING, no results published
updates.whatIsNew: NOT yet reported. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05702034, milvexian 25 mg twice daily after acute ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA, enrolment 12,523, status ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING, estimated primary completion 15 October 2026 (checked 29 Aug 2026). No primary-outcome publication and no conference presentation of primary results found. Phase 2 predecessors (PACIFIC-Stroke for asundexian, AXIOMATIC-SSP for milvexian) had neutral primary endpoints with reassuring safety. Sibling trials: LIBREXIA-ACS (NCT05754957) COMPLETED, primary completion 6 Feb 2026; LIBREXIA-AF (NCT05757869) ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING, primary completion 8 Dec 2026. Also note OCEANIC-AF was stopped for inferiority — asundexian vs apixaban in AF, stroke/systemic embolism 1.3% vs 0.4%, HR 3.79 (95% CI 2.46–5.83), despite less major bleeding (0.2% vs 0.7%, HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.18–0.55) — showing FXIa inhibition is indication-dependent and must not be extrapolated to AF. Best current narrative reference for the whole class in stroke, with the dosing-rationale paper: Weitz JI, Harrington RA; LIBREXIA Program Executive Council. Rationale for the milvexian dosing in the phase 3 LIBREXIA program. J Thromb Haemost. 2026;24(6):2158-69. doi:10.1016/j.jtha.2026.02.020.
updates.citation: Ferrari F, Villa RF. Factor XI inhibition for ischemic stroke secondary prevention: pharmacology, clinical evidence, and future directions. J Clin Pharmacol. 2026;66(8):e70266. doi:10.1002/jcph.70266.

updates.topic: PASCAL classification — definitive validation in the SCOPE individual-participant-data meta-analysis of all 6 PFO closure RCTs
updates.whatIsNew: The document names PASCAL twice but gives no validating data. This analysis supplies them. All 6 randomised trials of transcatheter PFO closure vs antithrombotic therapy, 3,740 patients (1,889 closure, 1,851 medical), mean age 45 (SD 10) years. PASCAL classified PFO relatedness as probable in 1,382 (37.0%), possible in 1,811 (48.4%), unlikely in 547 (14.6%); in the 4 broad-entry trials (n=2,967) probable 860 (29.0%), possible 1,565 (52.7%), unlikely 543 (18.3%). Net benefit over 5 years, absolute stroke reduction vs absolute increase in first-ever post-periprocedural (>45 days) AF: probable −2.5% strokes (95% CI −4.2% to −1.3%) vs +1.3% late AF (95% CI 0.0% to 2.5%); possible −3.4% strokes (95% CI −5.4% to −1.3%) vs +1.1% late AF (95% CI −0.5% to 2.6%); unlikely NO stroke reduction (+0.4%, 95% CI −4.0% to 4.8%) with magnified late AF (+4.6%, 95% CI 0.3% to 8.9%). Conclusion: PASCAL separates the 4 in 5 patients with net benefit from the 1 in 5 with net harm. This is the strongest available justification for making PASCAL, not RoPE alone, the operational selection tool in section 4.2.3/4.2.4.
updates.citation: Saver JL, Kent DM, Kasner SE, Koethe B, Carroll JD, Chatellier G, et al. Patent foramen ovale closure in stroke and the PASCAL classification system. JAMA Neurol. 2026;83(3):242-9. doi:10.1001/jamaneurol.2025.5446.

updates.topic: PFO closure beyond age 60 — systematic review and meta-analysis (the only synthesis available)
updates.whatIsNew: Directly fills the document's acknowledged gap ('Dữ liệu chưa đủ để khuyến cáo thường quy ngoài nhóm tuổi này'). Searched Jan 2004–Jul 2025; only ONE randomised source (a post hoc evaluation of DEFENSE-PFO) plus 11 observational studies — the evidence base is predominantly non-randomised. In patients ≥60 years, PFO closure vs antithrombotic therapy alone: recurrent stroke 5.48% vs 10.05%, HR 0.56 (95% CI 0.45–0.80), p<0.001, I²=45.6%; all-cause mortality 1.73% vs 7.59%, HR 0.41 (95% CI 0.19–0.90), p=0.02, I²=43.8%; new-onset AF HR 1.13 (95% CI 0.53–2.44), p=0.74. Comparing ≥60 vs <60 years AFTER closure: recurrent stroke 2.94% vs 1.04%, HR 3.47 (95% CI 1.61–7.48), p=0.001; new-onset AF 4.86% vs 1.01%, HR 4.12 (95% CI 1.90–8.95), p<0.001; all-cause mortality 8.32% vs 0.39%, HR 8.24 (95% CI 3.49–19.46), p<0.0001. In-hospital complications comparable across age groups. PROSPERO CRD420250652870. Authors explicitly warn of selection bias and unmeasured confounding and state randomised trials remain essential.
updates.citation: Jazayeri SB, Phan C, Ghozy S, Ravichandran S, Maleki AH, Dumitrascu OM, et al. Outcomes of patent foramen ovale closure in patients over 60 years with cryptogenic stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Int J Stroke. 2026;21(5):603-12. doi:10.1177/17474930251392333.

updates.topic: PFO closure beyond age 60 — the two ongoing randomised trials (registry records, no results)
updates.whatIsNew: Neither has reported; both should be named in the 'câu hỏi mở'/future-directions section (4.4), which currently lists no PFO trial at all. (1) CLOSE-2, NCT05387954, Assistance Publique–Hôpitaux de Paris: 'Transcatheter PFO closure, oral anticoagulants or antiplatelet therapy after PFO-associated stroke in patients between 60 and 80 years old'. Three-arm randomised trial, ages 60–80, requires large shunt (>20 microbubbles) or PFO with atrial septal aneurysm (>10 mm) plus otherwise unexplained ischaemic stroke; estimated n=792; primary outcome time to recurrent stroke (ischaemic or haemorrhagic, fatal or non-fatal); actual start 7 Jul 2023; estimated primary completion 7 Jul 2031; status RECRUITING as of 29 Aug 2026. (2) STOP, NCT05907694, PI Josep Rodés-Cabau: 'Medical treatment with or without transcatheter PFO closure for older patients with cryptogenic stroke and PFO'. Inclusion requires age >60 with TEE-documented right-to-left shunt; estimated n=714; primary outcome rate of ischaemic events at 12 months; actual start 18 Jun 2024; estimated primary completion 1 Oct 2027; status RECRUITING. Until these read out, any closure offered above 60 remains outside randomised evidence.
updates.citation: CLOSE-2: Assistance Publique - Hôpitaux de Paris. Transcatheter patent foramen ovale (PFO) closure, oral anticoagulants or antiplatelet therapy after PFO-associated stroke in patients between 60 and 80 years old: a randomised controlled trial. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT05387954. Bethesda (MD): National Library of Medicine (US); 2022 [cited 2026 Aug 29]. Available from: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05387954. STOP: Rodés-Cabau J. Medical treatment with or without transcatheter patent foramen ovale closure for older patients with cryptogenic stroke and patent foramen ovale: the STOP trial. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT05907694. Bethesda (MD): National Library of Medicine (US); 2023 [cited 2026 Aug 29]. Available from: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05907694.

updates.topic: ESO 2024 PFO guideline — two details the document omits and one it slightly overstates
updates.whatIsNew: Reference 70 is already cited and its volume/pages/DOI are correct (verified). But the document's summary at section 4.2.3 misses two points that matter for a TIA/minor-stroke monograph. (a) TIA WAS DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED as an index event: the guideline states 'Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA) was not considered an index event in this context because only one RCT involved TIA patients', although the subgroup analysis showed no significant difference between TIA and stroke outcomes. For a doctoral thesis on TIA this is a material limitation of the PFO evidence base and should be stated explicitly. (b) The guideline gives LOW-quality evidence SUGGESTING AGAINST closure in patients classified PASCAL-unlikely, except in specific scenarios (Expert Consensus) — a negative recommendation the document does not carry. (c) The guideline also notes it found no validated diagnostic algorithm for PFO detection and that TOE's status as gold standard 'remains unsubstantiated by rigorously validated evidence' — relevant to section 4.2.4. Confirmed as written: high-quality evidence for closure plus antiplatelet in selected 18–60-year-olds; PASCAL may be used to select candidates; greatest benefit with both large right-to-left shunt and atrial septal aneurysm; insufficient evidence for >60 and <18 years; suggests against long-term anticoagulation unless otherwise indicated; substantial uncertainty about long-term AF monitoring (e.g. implantable loop recorders) after closure.
updates.citation: Caso V, Turc G, Abdul-Rahim AH, Castro P, Hussain S, Lal A, et al. European Stroke Organisation (ESO) guidelines on the diagnosis and management of patent foramen ovale (PFO) after stroke. Eur Stroke J. 2024;9(4):800-34. doi:10.1177/23969873241247978.

updates.topic: ARCADIA — the primary result is correctly reported, but the bleeding row in Bảng 4.5 is wrong
updates.whatIsNew: Verified primary publication: 1,015 of a target 1,100 enrolled, mean follow-up 1.8 years, stopped for futility at planned interim analysis; mean age 68.0 (SD 11.0), 54.3% female. Recurrent stroke 40 vs 40 patients, annualised 4.4% vs 4.4%, HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.64–1.55) — the document's numbers match but omit the CI, which should be added because it is wide enough to exclude only large effects. CORRECTION NEEDED: the document's Bảng 4.5 records bleeding as 'Tương đương'. In fact symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage occurred in 0 apixaban patients vs 7 aspirin patients (annualised 1.1%); other major haemorrhages 5 vs 5 (annualised 0.7% vs 0.8%), HR 1.02 (95% CI 0.29–3.52). Apixaban was not simply 'equivalent' — it caused fewer intracranial bleeds, which changes the interpretive framing of the trial.
updates.citation: Kamel H, Longstreth WT Jr, Tirschwell DL, Kronmal RA, Marshall RS, Broderick JP, et al. Apixaban to prevent recurrence after cryptogenic stroke in patients with atrial cardiopathy: the ARCADIA randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2024;331(7):573-81. doi:10.1001/jama.2023.27188.

updates.topic: ARCADIA secondary analysis — bleeding profile (confirms the correction above)
updates.whatIsNew: Dedicated haemorrhage analysis of all 1,015 randomised patients, mean follow-up 1.8 (SD 1.2) years. 115 patients (11.3%) had 146 haemorrhages: 27 (18.5%) major, 119 (81.5%) minor. Apixaban produced significantly FEWER intracranial haemorrhages than aspirin in both the safety sample (incidence rate difference −1.4%, 95% CI −2.3% to −0.5%) and the intention-to-treat sample (IRD −1.0%, 95% CI −1.8% to −0.2%). Symptomatic ICH in the safety sample IRD −1.1% (95% CI −1.8% to −0.3%), not significant in ITT (IRD −0.7%, 95% CI −1.4% to 0.0%, p=0.11). No difference in major non-intracranial, any major, or minor haemorrhage. This is the citable basis for stating that ARCADIA's neutrality was driven by lack of efficacy, not by bleeding harm.
updates.citation: Kamel H, Longstreth WT Jr, Tirschwell DL, Kronmal RA, Elkind MSV, Pauls Q, et al. Apixaban versus aspirin and risk of hemorrhage in the ARCADIA trial. Ann Neurol. 2026;99(6):1589-97. doi:10.1002/ana.78186.

updates.topic: ARCADIA-MRI — apixaban DID reduce covert (silent) infarcts
updates.whatIsNew: The single most interpretation-changing ARCADIA secondary analysis, and it cuts against the document's flat statement that atrial cardiopathy biomarkers are useless for selecting anticoagulation. ARCADIA-MRI enrolled 310 of the 1,015 ARCADIA participants (31%) at 75 US sites (Nov 2019–Dec 2022); 174 (56% of those enrolled) had adequate baseline and follow-up MRI. Mean age 66 (SD 10.6), median mRS 1 (IQR 0–2), 52.3% male. Over median follow-up 811 days (IQR 487–1288), incident non-lacunar covert infarct occurred in 5.1% of the apixaban arm (n=79) vs 17.9% of the aspirin arm (n=95); weighted relative risk 0.29 (95% CI 0.10–0.83). Caveats to state: small subset, MRI surrogate endpoint, no effect on clinical recurrence in the parent trial. Companion editorial: JAMA Neurol. 2025;82(3):214-5. doi:10.1001/jamaneurol.2024.4847.
updates.citation: Lansberg MG, Wintermark M, Chen H, Howard G, Cassarly C, Pauls Q, et al. Apixaban to prevent covert infarcts after cryptogenic stroke in patients with atrial cardiopathy: a secondary analysis of the ARCADIA randomized clinical trial. JAMA Neurol. 2025;82(3):220-7. doi:10.1001/jamaneurol.2024.4838.

updates.topic: ARCADIA — why the atrial cardiopathy biomarkers may have failed: their predictive performance for incident AF
updates.whatIsNew: Provides the mechanistic explanation the document asserts but does not evidence. Of 3,745 patients consenting to screening for atrial cardiopathy, 254 were subsequently diagnosed with AF (96 before randomisation, 158 after). Unadjusted: ln(NT-proBNP) RR per SD 1.99 (95% CI 1.85–2.13); P-wave terminal force in V1 (PTFV1) RR per SD 1.15 (95% CI 1.03–1.28); left atrial diameter index (LADI) RR per SD 1.34 (95% CI 1.20–1.50). In a model with all three biomarkers plus demographics and AF risk factors, only age (RR per 10 years 1.24, 95% CI 1.09–1.41), ln(NT-proBNP) (RR per SD 1.88, 95% CI 1.67–2.11) and LADI (RR per SD 1.25, 95% CI 1.14–1.37) remained associated; c-statistic 0.82 (95% CI 0.79–0.85) with only modest calibration. Conclusion: the ARCADIA biomarkers were only moderately predictive of AF — notably PTFV1 dropped out. Accompanying commentary: Acampa M, Lazzerini PE. Searching for biomarkers of atrial cardiomyopathy at high risk of cardioembolism: what are the missing pieces of the puzzle? Eur Stroke J. 2025;10(2):502-3. doi:10.1177/23969873241276357. ARCADIA thresholds for the thesis: PTFV1 >5000 μV·ms in V1, NT-proBNP >250 pg/mL, or LADI ≥3 cm/m².
updates.citation: Kamel H, Elkind MS, Kronmal RA, Longstreth WT Jr, Plummer P, Aragon Garcia R, et al. Atrial cardiopathy biomarkers and atrial fibrillation in the ARCADIA trial. Eur Stroke J. 2025;10(2):495-501. doi:10.1177/23969873241276358.

updates.topic: ARCADIA — hypertensive arteriopathy as an explanation for ESUS anticoagulation trial failures
updates.whatIsNew: Exploratory but conceptually important and highly citable for section 4.1's discussion of ESUS phenotyping. Among 945 patients (mean age 68.0, SD 10.8; 513 [54.3%] female), 351 (37.1%) met criteria for hypertension with high-risk features. Median follow-up 1.6 years (IQR 0.7–3.0); 67 recurrent ischaemic strokes or systemic emboli. A significant treatment interaction was found: in the 594 patients WITHOUT hypertension with high-risk features, apixaban was associated with lower risk than aspirin — HR 0.43 (95% CI 0.22–0.85), annualised rate difference −3.4%; in those WITH such hypertension, no benefit — HR 1.68 (95% CI 0.78–3.62), annualised rate difference +2.4%. The authors propose that unrecognised inclusion of strokes due to hypertensive arteriopathy may explain the null results across the ESUS anticoagulation programme. Must be labelled exploratory/hypothesis-generating.
updates.citation: Ridha M, Hailat R, Stanton R, Merkler AE, Elkind MSV, Longstreth WT Jr, et al. Hypertension with high-risk features in cryptogenic stroke: an exploratory analysis of the ARCADIA randomized clinical trial. JAMA Neurol. 2026;83(6):573-81. doi:10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.0855.

updates.topic: ARCADIA — left ventricular systolic dysfunction as a candidate responder phenotype
updates.whatIsNew: Post hoc analysis with central echocardiography core-lab review from 185 US and Canadian sites. Of 964 patients with complete echo data (of 1,015 enrolled), 165 (17.1%) had LV systolic dysfunction (defined as fractional shortening <25%, LVEF <50%, or any wall motion abnormality; mean age 67, 43% female, mean follow-up 1.7 years) and 799 (82.9%) did not. Recurrent ischaemic stroke was numerically more frequent with LV dysfunction (15, 9.1%) than without (50, 6.3%), but LV dysfunction was not independently associated with recurrence after adjustment (HR 1.3, 95% CI 0.7–2.4). Treatment interaction: apixaban vs aspirin HR 0.24 (95% CI 0.07–0.87) in patients WITH LV systolic dysfunction vs HR 1.13 (95% CI 0.65–1.96) WITHOUT; P for interaction = 0.028. Together with the hypertension analysis this supports the document's own thesis (line 581–582) that ESUS needs mechanism-based phenotyping rather than a single anticoagulant for all — but the document currently states this without any supporting subgroup data.
updates.citation: Sharma R, Jillella D, Zhang C, Elkind MSV, Kamel H, Di Tullio MR, et al. Apixaban and recurrent stroke risk with left ventricular dysfunction: a secondary analysis of the ARCADIA trial. Stroke. 2025;56(11):3118-26. doi:10.1161/STROKEAHA.125.052724.

updates.topic: ARCADIA — multiterritory infarction as a risk marker that anticoagulation does not modify
updates.whatIsNew: Among 3,464 screened patients with reported baseline MRI data: 220 (6.4%) no visible acute infarct, 2,794 (80.7%) infarction in 1 territory, 374 (10.8%) in 2, 76 (2.2%) in 3. Atrial cardiopathy biomarkers and LVEF were NOT associated with the number of infarcted territories. Among the 937 of these who were randomised, recurrent stroke risk rose with territory count: 2 territories HR 2.4 (95% CI 1.3–4.2), 3 territories HR 3.7 (95% CI 1.5–9.3) vs single-territory; absence of visible infarction not associated (HR 1.8, 95% CI 0.6–4.9). Crucially, territory count did NOT modify the apixaban vs aspirin effect (P for interaction 0.71). Directly relevant to the document's Hình 2.5 / section 2.4.2 claim that multi-territory lesions should prompt a hypercoagulable workup — they predict recurrence but do not identify anticoagulation responders.
updates.citation: Gologorsky R, Lansberg MG, Wintermark M, Cassarly CN, Aragon Garcia R, Plummer P, et al. Multiterritory brain infarcts, anticoagulation, and recurrence after cryptogenic stroke: a subgroup analysis of the ARCADIA trial. Stroke. 2026;57(3):570-6. doi:10.1161/STROKEAHA.125.053079.

updates.topic: ARCADIA — cancer subgroup (relevant to the document's cancer-associated hypercoagulability discussion)
updates.whatIsNew: Among 1,015 participants (median age 68, IQR 60–76; 551 [54.3%] female), 137 (13.5%) had a history of cancer; median follow-up 1.5 years in both groups. History of cancer conferred higher risk of major ischaemic or major haemorrhagic events, HR 1.73 (95% CI 1.10–2.71). Within the cancer subgroup, events occurred in 8 of 61 (13.1%) randomised to apixaban vs 16 of 76 (21.1%) randomised to aspirin, HR 0.61 (95% CI 0.26–1.43) — not significant. Component events, apixaban vs aspirin: recurrent stroke 5 (8.2%) vs 9 (11.8%); major ischaemic events 7 (11.5%) vs 14 (18.4%); major haemorrhagic events 1 (1.6%) vs 2 (2.6%). Supports the document's statement (line 337) that cancer-associated hypercoagulability is an ESUS mechanism to hunt, while showing that empirical apixaban is not established therapy for it.
updates.citation: Navi BB, Zhang C, Miller B, Cushman M, Kasner SE, Elkind MSV, et al. Apixaban vs aspirin in patients with cancer and cryptogenic stroke: a post hoc analysis of the ARCADIA randomized clinical trial. JAMA Neurol. 2024;81(9):958-65. doi:10.1001/jamaneurol.2024.2404.

updates.topic: ARCADIA-Cognition — no cognitive benefit from apixaban
updates.whatIsNew: Of 799 screened at 75 sites, 310 enrolled in ARCADIA-CSI; 296 completed at least one cognitive exam; 47 excluded for baseline dementia, leaving 249 analysed (128 apixaban, 121 aspirin) with 582 cognitive assessments. Mean age 68 (SD 10.4), median mRS 1 (IQR 0–2), 52% female, 19% Black. Median follow-up 378 days (IQR 183–735). Annual change in overall standardised composite z-score: aspirin 0.084 (95% CI 0.017–0.149) vs apixaban 0.107 (95% CI 0.041–0.174), P=0.62. No difference in cognitive trajectory. Useful because the document raises atrial cardiopathy as a future personalised-medicine axis (line 656) — this closes off the cognitive-protection rationale.
updates.citation: Lazar RM, Howard G, Brewer MT, Cassarly C, Pauls Q, Kemp S, et al. Apixaban versus aspirin to reduce cognitive decline after cryptogenic stroke and atrial cardiopathy: ARCADIA-Cognition study. J Am Heart Assoc. 2025;14(18):e042147. doi:10.1161/JAHA.125.042147.

updates.topic: Atrial cardiopathy in ESUS — large East Asian real-world cohort (directly relevant to the Vietnamese population argument)
updates.whatIsNew: The document repeatedly argues that Western-derived evidence needs adaptation for East Asian populations; this is the corresponding atrial-cardiopathy dataset. Korean multicentre stroke registries 2014–2019, 5,787 patients aged ≥20 with acute ESUS or cardiogenic stroke without a definite embolic source (mean age 65.9 ± 13.9; 39.8% female). Atrial cardiopathy defined as LA enlargement (diameter >40 mm men, >38 mm women, or LA volume index >34 mL/m²) OR NT-proBNP ≥250 pg/mL; 45.0% met criteria (group 1, one factor: 40.3%; group 2, both factors: 4.7%). Original cohort: group 2 associated with recurrence HR 1.76 (95% CI 1.06–2.92), P=0.03. After propensity-score matching: any atrial cardiopathy HR 1.37 (95% CI 1.04–1.79), P=0.02; group 2 HR 1.94 (95% CI 1.16–3.26), P=0.01; MACE in group 2 HR 1.70 (95% CI 1.07–2.70), P=0.02. Neither NT-proBNP alone (HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.84–1.12, P=0.69) nor LA enlargement alone (HR 1.15, 95% CI 0.89–1.49, P=0.28) was predictive. Key message: atrial cardiopathy is prognostic (identifies higher-risk ESUS) even though ARCADIA showed it is not predictive of anticoagulation benefit — a distinction the document does not currently draw.
updates.citation: Kim SH, Kim HJ, Kim HK, Baek JH, Kim HY, Hwang YH, et al. Atrial cardiopathy worsens neurological severity, raises recurrence rates, and leads to poor vascular outcomes in patients with embolic stroke of undetermined source. J Stroke. 2025;27(3):350-9. doi:10.5853/jos.2025.00906.

updates.topic: Atrial cardiopathy biomarkers — new imaging marker: left atrial to left ventricular volume ratio
updates.whatIsNew: Proposes a replacement for indexed left atrial volume (LAVi), which the document lists as a standard atrial-cardiopathy marker. Two cohorts: UK Biobank population cohort n=38,848 and University Hospital Zürich ischaemic stroke cohort n=1,273. In UK Biobank, LAVi was NOT significantly associated with incident ischaemic stroke/TIA (adjusted HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.97–1.26, P=0.14), whereas a larger LA:LV ratio was (adjusted HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.01–1.30, P=0.04); LA:LV was also more strongly associated with worse cognitive function. In the stroke cohort, LA:LV outperformed LAVi at identifying AF/flutter as the underlying cause: AUC 0.856 (95% CI 0.803–0.908) vs 0.808 (95% CI 0.750–0.866), P=0.03. Rationale: LAVi is confounded by physiological remodelling (e.g. exercise); the ratio detects imbalanced pathological atrial remodelling. Still a single (albeit large) two-cohort study — present as promising, not established.
updates.citation: Deseoe J, Hänsel M, Herzog L, Davoudi N, Luft AR, Gebhard C, et al. Ratio of left atrial and ventricular volume as new marker of atrial cardiopathy and stroke risk. Stroke. 2026;57(8):2426-36. doi:10.1161/STROKEAHA.126.055551.

updates.topic: Atrial cardiopathy biomarkers — left atrial strain combined with NT-proBNP in cryptogenic stroke
updates.whatIsNew: Small prospective single-centre Spanish study, 136 patients: 44 cardioembolic stroke due to AF, 52 non-cardioembolic, 40 cryptogenic. The combination of NT-proBNP ≥469 pg/mL with biplanar left atrial strain during the contraction phase (LASct) ≥ −10.2% was the best-performing biomarker combination for identifying cardioembolic aetiology, AUC 0.995. Applying the derived logistic model, 30% of cryptogenic-stroke patients had a predicted atrial-cardiopathy probability >0.5; these were older (77.3 ± 8 vs 68.8 ± 10 years, p=0.011), had more severe strokes (NIHSS 10.1 ± 7.5 vs 4.6 ± 5.2, p=0.024) and more incident AF during follow-up (6 vs 0 cases, p=0.029). Important caveats for the thesis: very small sample, single centre, AUC 0.995 is almost certainly optimistic (derivation without external validation). Include only as an emerging-technique signal, not as validated practice.
updates.citation: López-Dequidt I, Eiras-Penas S, González-Maestro A, Peña-Gil C, Rodríguez-Castro E, Santamaría-Cadavid M, et al. Multiparametric assessment of atrial cardiopathy in cryptogenic stroke patients: implications for personalized clinical management. Eur Stroke J. 2026;11(1):23969873251372773. doi:10.1093/esj/23969873251372773.

updates.topic: PASCAL and RoPE — external validation in long-term real-world cohorts
updates.whatIsNew: Two independent registries confirm that PASCAL and RoPE predict recurrence after closure, complementing the SCOPE randomised analysis. (1) Vienna single-centre cohort, 330 patients closed 2010–2015, mean age 49 ± 12, 55.5% male, 86% index stroke, 19% multiple prior neurological events. Procedure-related complications 2.4%. Over median 10 years, combined endpoint (TIA, stroke or death from stroke) in 3.6%; recurrence 0.38 per 100 patient-years; freedom from endpoint 97.5% at 5 years and 96.2% at 10 years; new-onset AF 3%. Independent predictors of recurrence: RoPE score (adjusted HR 0.68, p=0.032), PASCAL classification (adjusted HR 0.37, p=0.042), prior neurological events (adjusted HR 9.94, p<0.001). Age, sex and cardiovascular risk factors did not influence outcomes. (2) PROLONG registry, 12 Italian centres, 1,245 patients closed 1999–2013 for cryptogenic embolism, mean age 47 ± 12, 56% women, mean follow-up 14.5 ± 2.4 years. Recurrent stroke/TIA/systemic embolism in 34 (2.7%), 0.19 per 100 patient-years. Predictors: RoPE ≤7 (HR 3.44, 95% CI 1.06–11.3, P=0.041), non-probable PASCAL (HR 2.72, 95% CI 1.17–6.34, P=0.020), new-onset AF (HR 7.01, 95% CI 2.45–20.1, P<0.001). Serious complications 0.4% in hospital and 0.4% during follow-up, all non-fatal. NCT06504121.

Int J Stroke. 2025;20(4):450-60. doi:10.1177/17474930241298778. AND Gaspardone C, Trabattoni D, d'Atri DO, Morosato M, Costa P, Fraccaro C, et al. 15-year outcomes of PFO closure in patients with cryptogenic embolism: insights from the PROLONG registry. JACC Cardiovasc Interv. 2025;18(12):1526-37. doi:10.1016/j.jcin.2025.04.041.

updates.topic: PFO and stroke — current authoritative narrative review with pooled trial estimates (useful single citation for section 4.2)
updates.whatIsNew: Provides quotable pooled numbers the document currently lacks. PFO present in ~25% of all adults; paradoxical embolism accounts for ~5% of all strokes and ~10% of strokes in younger patients. Approximately 50% of patients aged ≤60 with ESUS have a PFO vs 25% of the general population — this SUPPORTS but refines the document's '40–50%' figure at line 585. RoPE calibration: in the lowest RoPE category (score <3) PFO prevalence was 23%, essentially that of the general population; at RoPE 9–10, PFO prevalence was 77%. Pooled analysis of 6 trials (3,740 patients), median follow-up 57 months: annualised stroke 0.47% (95% CI 0.35%–0.65%) with closure vs 1.09% (95% CI 0.88%–1.36%) with medical therapy, adjusted HR 0.41 (95% CI 0.28–0.60). In PASCAL 'probable' patients, 90% relative reduction in recurrent ischaemic stroke at 2 years, HR 0.10 (95% CI 0.03–0.35), absolute risk reduction 2.1% (95% CI 0.9%–3.4%). PASCAL 'unlikely' patients had no stroke reduction but higher procedure- and device-related adverse events including AF. Note an erratum is recorded (JAMA. 2025;334(9):833. doi:10.1001/jama.2025.14546).
updates.citation: Kent DM, Wang AY. Patent foramen ovale and stroke: a review. JAMA. 2025;334(16):1463-73. doi:10.1001/jama.2025.10946.

updates.topic: PFO closure at ≥60 years — nationwide Swedish registry (safety signal, counterpoint to the meta-analysis)
updates.whatIsNew: All adult Swedish patients with cryptogenic stroke treated with percutaneous PFO closure 2001–2023, from the Swedish registry of adult congenital heart disease linked to national diagnosis registries. 1,101 patients, follow-up 7.1 ± 5.8 years; 134 (12%) were ≥60 years. No difference in AF within 3 months of closure (≥60 years: 4 patients, 3.0%; <60 years: 23 patients, 2.4%; p=0.229) and no difference in recurrent cerebral infarction/TIA (≥60: 3, 2.7%; <60: 17, 1.5%; p=0.697). Authors conclude closure can be considered safe and effective in patients over 60 WITH LOW PREPROCEDURAL COMORBIDITY — an important qualifier, and one that conflicts with the higher AF and mortality hazards in older patients reported in the Jazayeri meta-analysis. Worth presenting as an unresolved discrepancy pending CLOSE-2 and STOP.
updates.citation: Damlin A, Verouhis D, Settergren M. Percutaneous closure of patent foramen ovale after cryptogenic stroke - a comparison between patients < 60 versus ≥ 60 years-of-age. Cardiovasc Interv Ther. 2026;41(3):816-25. doi:10.1007/s12928-026-01269-z.

updates.topic: ATTICUS — citation and numbers verified as correct in the document
updates.whatIsNew: No change needed, but confirming since the document reports it. Verified: 352 patients randomised (178 apixaban 5 mg twice daily, 174 aspirin 100 mg once daily), initiated within 28 days of ESUS at a median of 8 days. Eligibility required at least one predictive factor for atrial fibrillation OR a patent foramen ovale (the document says 'kèm yếu tố nguy cơ tim', which omits the PFO limb of the entry criterion and should be corrected). Cardiac monitoring was mandatory and aspirin was switched to apixaban on AF detection. MRI follow-up available in 325 (92.3%). Primary outcome, any new ischaemic lesion on MRI at 12 months: 23 of 169 (13.6%) apixaban vs 25 of 156 (16.0%) aspirin, adjusted OR 0.79 (95% CI 0.42–1.48), P=0.57 — matches the document exactly. Major and clinically relevant non-major bleeding in 5 and 7 participants (1-year cumulative incidences 2.9 and 4.2), HR 0.68 (95% CI 0.22–2.16). Terminated for futility at prespecified interim analysis. NCT02427126.
updates.citation: Geisler T, Keller T, Martus P, Poli K, Serna-Higuita LM, Schreieck J, et al. Apixaban versus aspirin for embolic stroke of undetermined source. NEJM Evid. 2024;3(1):EVIDoa2300235. doi:10.1056/EVIDoa2300235.

updates.topic: Lipid lowering after stroke — how low to go (FOURIER/FOURIER-OLE prior-ischaemic-stroke analysis)
updates.whatIsNew: In 5,291 FOURIER/FOURIER-OLE participants with a prior ischaemic stroke (>4 weeks), risk fell monotonically with lower achieved LDL-C (Ptrend <0.001 primary endpoint; 0.002 all stroke; 0.002 ischaemic stroke). Versus LDL-C >=70 mg/dL, those achieving <40 mg/dL had incidence rate ratios of 0.69 (95% CI 0.57-0.84) for the primary endpoint, 0.73 (95% CI 0.53-0.99) for all stroke and 0.75 (95% CI 0.54-1.05) for ischaemic stroke. Haemorrhagic strokes were infrequent and unrelated to achieved LDL-C (Ptrend=0.85). Median follow-up 2.2 y in FOURIER plus a further 5 y in the open-label extension. This is the strongest post-2020 evidence that in stroke patients 'lower is better' extends below the <70 and even <55 mg/dL thresholds without a haemorrhagic penalty.
updates.citation: Monguillon V, Kelly PJ, O'Donoghue ML, Park JG, Bohula EA, Saver JL, et al. Efficacy and safety of very low achieved LDL cholesterol in patients with previous ischemic stroke. Circulation. 2026;153(2):86-93. doi:10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.125.077549.

updates.topic: Timing of high-intensity statin after minor stroke / high-risk TIA (INSPIRES statin arm)
updates.whatIsNew: The statin arm of INSPIRES (2x2 factorial, 222 Chinese hospitals, N=6,100, mild ischaemic stroke NIHSS<=5 or high-risk TIA of atherosclerotic origin within 72 h) compared immediate-intensive statin with 3-day-delayed intensive statin. New stroke within 90 days: 245/3,050 (8.1%) vs 256/3,050 (8.4%), HR 0.95 (95% CI 0.80-1.13) — NEUTRAL for the primary endpoint. Poor functional outcome was less frequent with immediate treatment: 299 (9.8%) vs 348 (11.4%), OR 0.83 (95% CI 0.71-0.98). Moderate-to-severe bleeding 0.8% vs 0.6%. The document already uses INSPIRES for the antiplatelet arm (line 400, 413, 632) but never mentions the statin arm, while its lipid ladder asserts 'start high-intensity statin within 24-48 h' (line 438) without trial support. INSPIRES is the direct evidence for that step and it is neutral on recurrence.
updates.citation: Gao Y, Jiang L, Pan Y, Chen W, Jing J, Wang C, et al. Immediate- or delayed-intensive statin in acute cerebral ischemia: the INSPIRES randomized clinical trial. JAMA Neurol. 2024;81(7):741-751. doi:10.1001/jamaneurol.2024.1433.

updates.topic: Colchicine after non-cardioembolic stroke / high-risk TIA (CONVINCE)
updates.whatIsNew: CONVINCE (randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint; 3,154 randomised, 3,144 in ITT) tested colchicine 0.5 mg/day plus usual care vs usual care alone after non-severe non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA. Primary composite (recurrent ischaemic stroke, MI, cardiac arrest, or hospitalisation for unstable angina): 153/1,569 (9.8%) vs 185/1,575 (11.7%); incidence 3.32 vs 3.92 per 100 person-years; HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.68-1.05), p=0.12 (significance threshold 0.048). The trial stopped before the planned 367 events (COVID-related budget constraints). CRP was lower on colchicine at 28 days and at 1, 2 and 3 years (p<0.05 at all timepoints); serious adverse events were similar. The document discusses colchicine only through CHANCE-3 (ref 129) and states colchicine 'is not standard therapy because CHANCE-3 missed its primary endpoint' (line 653) — CONVINCE is the second and complementary pillar of that argument (long-term vs 90-day, European vs Chinese, underpowered vs adequately powered) and is entirely absent.
updates.citation: Kelly P, Lemmens R, Weimar C, Walsh C, Purroy F, Barber M, et al. Long-term colchicine for the prevention of vascular recurrent events in non-cardioembolic stroke (CONVINCE): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2024;404(10448):125-133. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(24)00968-1.

updates.topic: Colchicine harm signal in symptomatic intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (CHANCE-3 prespecified subgroup)
updates.whatIsNew: Prespecified subgroup analysis of CHANCE-3 in 7,567 patients with baseline intracranial artery assessment. In patients WITH symptomatic intracranial artery stenosis (sICAS), 90-day recurrent stroke occurred in 141 (10.5%) on colchicine vs 115 (8.5%) on placebo — adjusted HR 1.30 (95% CI 1.01-1.69), p=0.04, i.e. HARM. Without sICAS: 4.2% vs 5.2%, adjusted HR 0.80 (95% CI 0.62-1.05), p=0.10; adjusted interaction p=0.01. The interaction was strongest in elderly patients: in elderly sICAS patients (n=1,648) adjusted HR 1.58 (95% CI 1.13-2.20), p<0.001. Diarrhoea was more frequent on colchicine in both strata. This matters directly for the monograph because section 3.5 already handles symptomatic intracranial stenosis 70-99% as a distinct group; a signal of net harm from colchicine in exactly that group is a safety point, not just a negative-efficacy point.
updates.citation: Li J, Jing J, Meng X, Shi FD, Gu HQ, Jin A, et al. Colchicine for preventing stroke in patients with and without intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis: a prespecified analysis of a randomized clinical trial. EClinicalMedicine. 2025;84:103226. doi:10.1016/j.eclinm.2025.103226.

updates.topic: Blood pressure target after stroke — intensive SBP <120 mmHg (ESPRIT main trial)
updates.whatIsNew: ESPRIT randomised 11,255 high-cardiovascular-risk hypertensive patients in China (including 3,022 with previous stroke and 4,359 with diabetes) to SBP <120 vs <140 mmHg, open-label with blinded outcomes. Achieved mean SBP 119.1 (SD 11.1) vs 134.8 (10.5) mmHg. Over a median 3.4 years, the primary composite (MI, revascularisation, HF hospitalisation, stroke, cardiovascular death) occurred in 547 (9.7%) vs 623 (11.1%), HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.78-0.99), p=0.028, with NO heterogeneity by history of stroke. Serious syncope was more frequent with intensive treatment (24 [0.4%] vs 8 [0.1%], HR 3.00, 95% CI 1.35-6.68); no difference in hypotension, electrolyte abnormality, injurious fall or AKI. The document's BP section (3.6.2, line 533) rests on PROGRESS (2001), SPRINT (2015) and SPS3 (2013) and explicitly says SPRINT 'needs caution when applied to stroke and TIA' — ESPRIT is the trial that removes exactly that caveat by enrolling a large prespecified prior-stroke stratum.
updates.citation: Liu J, Li Y, Ge J, Yan X, Zhang H, Zheng X, et al. Lowering systolic blood pressure to less than 120 mm Hg versus less than 140 mm Hg in patients with high cardiovascular risk with and without diabetes or previous stroke: an open-label, blinded-outcome, randomised trial. Lancet. 2024;404(10449):245-255. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01028-6.

updates.topic: Stroke-specific effects of intensive BP lowering (ESPRIT prespecified stroke analysis)
updates.whatIsNew: Prespecified secondary analysis of ESPRIT on stroke endpoints (11,255 randomised; 3,022 with prior stroke; mean SBP 119.1 vs 134.8 mmHg over 3.4 y). Any stroke: 262 (4.7%) vs 303 (5.4%), HR 0.86 (95% CI 0.73-1.02), p=0.083 — not significant. Ischaemic stroke: 243 (4.3%) vs 261 (4.6%), HR 0.93 (95% CI 0.78-1.11), p=0.423. Haemorrhagic stroke: 23 (0.4%) vs 45 (0.8%), HR 0.51 (95% CI 0.31-0.85), p=0.009 — halved. Landmark analysis: the stroke difference emerged only after 1 year; HR beyond 1 year 0.75 (95% CI 0.60-0.94), p=0.011. No subgroup interactions. The clean message for a TIA/minor-stroke monograph is that targeting <120 mmHg buys haemorrhagic-stroke prevention and a delayed overall benefit, not an immediate reduction in ischaemic recurrence — a nuance the document's flat 'BP control is the single most effective intervention' framing does not carry.
updates.citation: Li J, Lei L, Li Y, Zhang H, Yan X, Sun Y, et al. Effect of intensive blood pressure control on stroke: a prespecified secondary analysis of the ESPRIT trial. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2025;86(17):1405-1417. doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2025.07.055.

updates.topic: When to (re)start antihypertensives after acute ischaemic stroke (CATIS-2)
updates.whatIsNew: CATIS-2, 106 Chinese hospitals, 4,810 patients with acute ischaemic stroke within 24-48 h and SBP 140 to <220 mmHg, not thrombolysed: antihypertensive treatment started immediately vs withheld until day 8. Day-7 mean SBP 139.1 vs 150.9 mmHg (p<0.001); 54.6% vs 22.4% achieved <140/90 mmHg. Primary outcome (mRS >=3 or death at 90 days): 289 (12.0%) early vs 250 (10.5%) delayed, OR 1.18 (95% CI 0.98-1.41), p=0.08 — early treatment did NOT reduce, and numerically favoured delay. No difference in recurrent stroke or adverse events. The document (line 533) states BP treatment should begin 'within 24-72 hours after the acute state stabilises' with no supporting trial; CATIS-2 is the direct randomised test of that timing and does not support urgency.
updates.citation: Liu L, Xie X, Pan Y, Wang A, Wei Y, Liu J, et al. Early versus delayed antihypertensive treatment in patients with acute ischaemic stroke: multicentre, open label, randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2023;383:e076448. doi:10.1136/bmj-2023-076448.

updates.topic: Blood pressure guidelines superseding the 2017/2021 framework (2025 AHA/ACC, 2024 ESC, 2023 ESH)
updates.whatIsNew: Three guideline documents post-date everything the monograph cites for BP (it uses the 2021 AHA/ASA secondary-prevention guideline [ref 18] and the 2024 AHA/ASA primary-prevention guideline [ref 41]). (1) The 2025 AHA/ACC multisociety BP guideline (Hypertension 2025;82(10):e212-e316; also Circulation 2025;152(11):e114-e218, doi:10.1161/CIR.0000000000001356) replaces the 2017 guideline and keeps a <130/80 mmHg treatment target while adding PREVENT-based risk estimation. (2) The 2024 ESC guideline introduces the 'elevated blood pressure' category (120-139/70-89 mmHg) and a target systolic range of 120-129 mmHg. (3) The 2023 ESH guideline retains an office target <140/90 then <130/80 if tolerated. A comparative review of BP management specifically in stroke across these documents plus the 2025 JSH guideline is available (Koga M. Hypertens Res. 2026;49(3):984-987. doi:10.1038/s41440-025-02517-0). Because the divergence between ESC (120-129) and AHA/ACC (<130/80) is now the live controversy, a doctoral monograph claiming currency to August 2026 should state which framework it adopts.

J Hypertens. 2023;41(12):1874-2071. doi:10.1097/HJH.0000000000003480.

updates.topic: GLP-1 receptor agonist cardiovascular outcomes — SOUL (oral semaglutide)
updates.whatIsNew: SOUL randomised 9,650 patients aged >=50 with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 6.5-10.0%) and established ASCVD, CKD, or both, to once-daily oral semaglutide (max 14 mg) or placebo. Median follow-up 49.5 months. MACE (cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke): 579/4,825 (12.0%; 3.1/100 person-years) vs 668/4,825 (13.8%; 3.7/100 person-years), HR 0.86 (95% CI 0.77-0.96), p=0.006. Confirmatory secondary kidney outcomes were not significantly different. Serious adverse events 47.9% vs 50.3%. The document's Table 3.10 and section 3.6.2 recommend 'SGLT-2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist' at evidence Level I but cite no GLP-1 outcomes trial at all — only the 2021 and 2024 AHA guidelines. SOUL is the current anchor trial and adds an oral route relevant to Vietnamese practice.
updates.citation: McGuire DK, Marx N, Mulvagh SL, Deanfield JE, Inzucchi SE, Pop-Busui R, et al. Oral semaglutide and cardiovascular outcomes in high-risk type 2 diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2025;392(20):2001-2012. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2501006.

updates.topic: Semaglutide in ASCVD without diabetes (SELECT)
updates.whatIsNew: SELECT randomised 17,604 patients aged >=45 with preexisting cardiovascular disease, BMI >=27, and no diabetes to weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo; mean follow-up 39.8 months. Primary MACE: 569/8,803 (6.5%) vs 701/8,801 (8.0%), HR 0.80 (95% CI 0.72-0.90), p<0.001. Permanent discontinuation for adverse events 16.6% vs 8.2% (p<0.001). Important caveat for a stroke monograph: SELECT enrolled patients with prior MI, prior stroke or symptomatic PAD, but the composite benefit was carried largely by coronary events; the trial does not establish an independent reduction in recurrent stroke. Cite it as the evidence for GLP-1 therapy in non-diabetic ASCVD, not as stroke-specific evidence.
updates.citation: Lincoff AM, Brown-Frandsen K, Colhoun HM, Deanfield J, Emerson SS, Esbjerg S, et al. Semaglutide and cardiovascular outcomes in obesity without diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2023;389(24):2221-2232. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2307563.

updates.topic: SGLT2 inhibitors and stroke — the document's claim needs correction
updates.whatIsNew: The document states at line 534 and in Table 3.10 (line 544) that SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists both deliver 'reduced major cardiovascular events, reduced cerebral infarction, reduced heart failure and reduced cardiovascular death'. The stroke component of that claim is not supported for SGLT-2 inhibitors. A systematic review of 32 studies of antidiabetic therapy and ischaemic stroke concluded that GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, dulaglutide) and pioglitazone reduce stroke risk, whereas 'dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitors, sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors, and insulin do not seem to affect the incidence of stroke'. The SGLT-2 class benefit is on heart failure, cardiovascular death and renal outcomes, not stroke. Recommend rewording the table so that the stroke-reduction claim attaches to GLP-1 agonists (and pioglitazone, per IRIS) and the heart-failure/renal claim to SGLT-2 inhibitors.
updates.citation: Prentza V, Pavlidis G, Ikonomidis I, Pililis S, Lampsas S, Kountouri A, et al. Antidiabetic treatment and prevention of ischemic stroke: a systematic review. J Clin Med. 2024;13(19):5786. doi:10.3390/jcm13195786.

updates.topic: Inclisiran has no published cardiovascular outcomes trial (ORION-4, VICTORION-2P)
updates.whatIsNew: The document places inclisiran at Step 3 of its lipid ladder alongside PCSK9 monoclonals (line 437, Table 3.5 line 452) citing only the phase 3 LDL-lowering trials (ref 91, Ray KK, NEJM 2020). As of 29 August 2026 no cardiovascular outcomes trial of inclisiran has reported. ORION-4 (NCT03705234, 'A randomized trial assessing the effects of inclisiran on clinical outcomes among people with cardiovascular disease', N=16,124) is ACTIVE, NOT RECRUITING with primary completion listed as October 2026. VICTORION-2-PREVENT (NCT05030428, N=17,004) is ACTIVE, NOT RECRUITING with primary completion 10 May 2027; only its design paper is published. A 2026 stroke-specific lipid review states plainly that for inclisiran and bempedoic acid 'stroke-specific efficacy data are still pending'. The monograph should say explicitly that inclisiran's Step-3 placement rests on LDL-C lowering alone.
updates.citation: Steg PG, Goodman SG, Jukema JW, Martens P, Zirlik A, Bhatt DL, et al. Design of VICTORION-2 Prevent: a randomized double-blind, placebo-controlled trial assessing the impact of inclisiran on major adverse cardiovascular events. Am Heart J. 2026;300:107493. doi:10.1016/j.ahj.2026.107493. | ClinicalTrials.gov. NCT03705234 (ORION-4), status active not recruiting, primary completion 2026-10; NCT05030428 (VICTORION-2-PREVENT), status active not recruiting, primary completion 2027-05-10. Both accessed 29 August 2026.

updates.topic: Lipoprotein(a) — no outcomes trial has reported yet
updates.whatIsNew: The document mentions Lp(a) only as a risk marker to measure once (line 457). As of 29 August 2026 no Lp(a)-lowering cardiovascular outcomes trial has published results. Lp(a)HORIZON (pelacarsen, NCT04023552, N=8,323) is registered as COMPLETED with completion date 16 July 2026 and record last updated 28 August 2026, but no results are posted and no primary publication is indexed; a comprehensive review published 13 August 2026 states pelacarsen lowers Lp(a) by ~80% and that Lp(a)HORIZON results are 'due in late 2026'. OCEAN(a)-Outcomes (olpasiran, NCT05581303, N=7,297) has primary completion 31 March 2028; ACCLAIM-Lp(a) (lepodisiran, NCT06292013, N=17,300) has primary completion March 2029; muvalaplin's phase 3 MOVE-Lp(a) is under way. For a monograph current to August 2026, the correct statement is: measure Lp(a) once for risk stratification; no therapy targeting it has yet been shown to reduce events.

Design and rationale of Lp(a)HORIZON trial: assessing the effect of lipoprotein(a) lowering with pelacarsen on major cardiovascular events in patients with CVD and elevated Lp(a). Am Heart J. 2025;287:1-9. doi:10.1016/j.ahj.2025.03.019.

updates.topic: PCSK9 inhibition extended below the classic secondary-prevention population (VESALIUS-CV)
updates.whatIsNew: VESALIUS-CV randomised 12,257 patients with atherosclerosis or diabetes but WITHOUT prior myocardial infarction or stroke and LDL-C >=90 mg/dL to evolocumab 140 mg every 2 weeks or placebo; median follow-up 4.6 years. 3-point MACE (coronary death, MI, ischaemic stroke): 336 patients, 5-year Kaplan-Meier 6.2% vs 443, 8.0%; HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.65-0.86), p<0.001. 4-point MACE: 13.4% vs 16.2%, HR 0.81 (95% CI 0.73-0.89), p<0.001. No between-group difference in safety events. This is the largest new PCSK9 outcomes trial since ODYSSEY OUTCOMES and the newest large lipid RCT overall; its relevance to a TIA monograph is indirect (it excluded prior stroke by design) but it is the evidence that pushes PCSK9 inhibition earlier in the risk continuum and is the natural companion to the FOURIER prior-stroke analysis above.
updates.citation: Bohula EA, Marston NA, Bhatia AK, De Ferrari GM, Leiter LA, Nicolau JC, et al. Evolocumab in patients without a previous myocardial infarction or stroke. N Engl J Med. 2026;394(2):117-127. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2514428.

updates.topic: Colchicine after myocardial infarction — the negative anchor trial (CLEAR SYNERGY / OASIS 9)
updates.whatIsNew: CLEAR SYNERGY randomised 7,062 post-MI patients at 104 centres in 14 countries (2x2 factorial with spironolactone) to colchicine 0.5 mg daily or placebo, median follow-up 3 years. Primary composite (cardiovascular death, recurrent MI, stroke, unplanned ischaemia-driven revascularisation): 322/3,528 (9.1%) vs 327/3,534 (9.3%), HR 0.99 (95% CI 0.85-1.16), p=0.93. CRP was reduced (adjusted least-squares mean difference -1.28 mg/L, 95% CI -1.81 to -0.75) despite no clinical benefit. Diarrhoea 10.2% vs 6.6% (p<0.001); no excess serious infection. Relevance to the monograph: the document's line 653 argument that colchicine is not standard rests only on CHANCE-3; CLEAR SYNERGY shows the anti-inflammatory hypothesis also failed in the coronary population where COLCOT and LoDoCo2 had succeeded, which strengthens the argument considerably and reframes it as a class-level uncertainty rather than a stroke-specific null.
updates.citation: Jolly SS, d'Entremont MA, Lee SF, Mian R, Tyrwhitt J, Kedev S, et al. Colchicine in acute myocardial infarction. N Engl J Med. 2025;392(7):633-642. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2405922.

updates.topic: Who might still benefit from colchicine after stroke (CONVINCE atherosclerosis subgroup)
updates.whatIsNew: Post hoc analysis of all 3,144 CONVINCE participants stratified by presence of atherosclerosis (cervico-cranial/aortic plaque, coronary disease, PAD, or carotid revascularisation); 338 MACE over median 33.6 months. In the atherosclerosis stratum, MACE occurred in 105 (11.1%; 3.88 per 100 person-years) on colchicine vs 132 (14.2%; 4.83 per 100 person-years) on usual care, HR 0.83 (95% CI 0.64-1.07) — not significant. Non-atherosclerosis stratum HR 0.94 (95% CI 0.64-1.39); interaction p=0.60. Recurrent ischaemic stroke in the atherosclerosis stratum HR 0.76 (95% CI 0.56-1.05); interaction p=0.48. In the prespecified ON-TREATMENT analysis colchicine did reduce MACE in the atherosclerosis group, HR 0.76 (95% CI 0.58-0.99), but not without atherosclerosis (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.63-1.42); interaction p=0.37. The authors conclude that presence of atherosclerosis should be an inclusion criterion in future anti-inflammatory stroke trials. This supports the monograph's own thesis (line 649) that mechanism-selected populations, not unselected ones, are where interventions succeed.
updates.citation: McCabe JJ, Lemmens R, Purroy F, Walsh C, Weimar C, Czlonkowska A, et al. Colchicine for secondary prevention after stroke according to the presence of atherosclerosis. Stroke. 2026 Aug 20 [Epub ahead of print; no volume/pages assigned as of 29 Aug 2026]. doi:10.1161/STROKEAHA.126.056561.

updates.topic: Lipid management guidance written specifically for stroke (ILEP consensus and Int J Stroke review)
updates.whatIsNew: Two 2026 documents give stroke-specific lipid guidance the monograph currently lacks — it relies on the 2021 AHA/ASA guideline (ref 18) and the 2022 ESO pharmacological secondary-prevention guideline (ref 85). (1) The International Lipid Expert Panel consensus, produced with the ESC Council on Stroke, notes LDL-C contributes to nearly one-third of ischaemic strokes, that up to 40% of patients at risk of recurrent ischaemic stroke recur within five years, and that up to 40% of post-stroke patients receive NO lipid-lowering therapy; it argues for early upfront combination lipid-lowering therapy rather than sequential step-up. (2) A phenotype-guided review in Int J Stroke argues for ApoB-containing lipoprotein and Lp(a) based stratification rather than uniform LDL-C targets, and addresses lipid lowering after intracerebral haemorrhage and in cerebral amyloid angiopathy. Both directly bear on the monograph's four-step lipid ladder (line 438, Table 3.5), which is a sequential rather than upfront-combination strategy.
updates.citation: Banach M, Toth PP, Ahn HJ, Bielecka-Dabrowa A, Cicero AFG, Covic A, et al. Lipid management for primary and secondary stroke prevention consensus paper of the International Lipid Expert Panel (ILEP). Prog Cardiovasc Dis. 2026;94:78-110. doi:10.1016/j.pcad.2025.11.003. | Stefanou MI, Panagiotopoulos E, Liberopoulos E, Milionis H, Theodorou A, Katan M, et al. Dyslipidemia management in stroke prevention: an individualized approach. Int J Stroke. 2026;21(6):759-777. doi:10.1177/17474930261418388.

updates.topic: Early PCSK9 inhibition in acute ischaemic stroke — signal only, low certainty
updates.whatIsNew: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 studies (n=1,842) initiating a PCSK9 inhibitor during hospitalisation or within 14 days of acute ischaemic stroke onset: recurrent stroke/TIA RR 0.38 (95% CI 0.26-0.54; I2=45.5%; LOW certainty); all-cause mortality RR 0.48 (95% CI 0.30-0.77; I2=0%; low certainty); early neurological deterioration RR 0.56 (95% CI 0.36-0.88; I2=0%; low certainty); functional independence mRS<=2 at 90 days RR 1.31 (95% CI 1.15-1.50; I2=0%; VERY LOW certainty); LDL-C mean difference -0.91 mmol/L (95% CI -1.26 to -0.57; I2=93%). Certainty downgraded for risk of bias and imprecision. A separate PRISMA-guided systematic review of PCSK9 inhibitors specifically in patients with prior stroke/TIA found only FOURIER and ODYSSEY OUTCOMES plus five meta-analyses, with prior-stroke analyses 'directionally consistent, though underpowered for stroke-specific endpoints'. Present this as hypothesis-generating; the effect sizes are implausibly large for the certainty available and no dedicated stroke outcomes RCT of a PCSK9 inhibitor exists.
updates.citation: Hamzah KA, Kurmasha YH, Shweliya MA, Al-Shammari AS, Alsaadany KR, Nofal AA, et al. Impact of early use of PCSK9 inhibitors in acute ischemic stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Clin Pharmacol. 2026;82(4):103. doi:10.1007/s00228-026-04014-w. | Epelde F. PCSK9 inhibitors for secondary prevention in patients with prior stroke: a PRISMA-guided systematic review. Curr Neuropharmacol. 2026 Jul 25 [Epub ahead of print]. doi:10.2174/011570159X450809260715104225.

updates.topic: Oral PCSK9 inhibition — enlicitide approved July 2026
updates.whatIsNew: Enlicitide, a macrocyclic peptide that blocks the PCSK9/LDL-receptor interaction, was approved by the US FDA in July 2026 as the first ORAL PCSK9 inhibitor. In the phase 3 CORALreef Lipids and CORALreef HeFH trials, once-daily enlicitide lowered LDL-C by approximately 60%, sustained to 52 weeks, with adverse event rates broadly similar to placebo. Those trials measured LDL-C, not cardiovascular events; the CORALreef Outcomes trial is ongoing. Relevant to a Vietnamese monograph because an oral agent removes the injection and cold-chain barriers that limit PCSK9 monoclonals and inclisiran in practice, but it must be presented as LDL-C evidence only, with no outcomes data. Note this source is a secondary review article, not the CORALreef primary publications.
updates.citation: Sun Y, Gao J. Enlicitide: the first oral PCSK9 inhibitor approved for treatment of hypercholesterolemia. Drug Discov Ther. 2026 Aug 14 [Epub ahead of print; no volume/pages assigned as of 29 Aug 2026]. doi:10.5582/ddt.2026.01051.

updates.topic: Blood pressure lowering after intracerebral haemorrhage (RECAP-ICH)
updates.whatIsNew: Individual participant data meta-analysis of 4 eligible randomised trials, 2,944 participants with prior spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage, median follow-up 42 months, mean achieved systolic difference 11.2 mmHg (95% CI 10.7-11.7). First recurrent stroke of any type: 96/1,487 (6.5%) vs 152/1,457 (10.4%), adjusted HR 0.62 (95% CI 0.48-0.80), p=0.0002, driven by fewer recurrent intracerebral haemorrhages (33 [2.2%] vs 81 [5.6%], adjusted HR 0.39, 95% CI 0.26-0.59, p<0.0001). Serious adverse events 28.9% vs 33.0%. Effects consistent across subgroups including time since index event; estimated time to a 1% absolute benefit 6.1 months (95% CI 3.5-14.8). Marginal for a TIA/minor-stroke monograph since the population is haemorrhagic, but useful if the thesis contrasts ischaemic and haemorrhagic secondary prevention, and it complements the ESPRIT haemorrhagic-stroke finding above.
updates.citation: Wang X, Gao Y, Velasco MJ, Harris K, Li S, Li J, et al. Intensive blood pressure lowering after spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage for secondary stroke prevention (RECAP-ICH): a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis. Lancet Neurol. 2026;25(9):830-839. doi:10.1016/S1474-4422(26)00244-9.

updates.topic: Colchicine effect by ischaemic stroke subtype (CONVINCE prespecified secondary analysis)
updates.whatIsNew: Prespecified secondary analysis of CONVINCE in 3,100 of 3,154 patients by TOAST-style index-event aetiology. The treatment effect did not vary across stroke subtype (interaction p=0.64). Large-artery atherosclerosis: primary endpoint in 32/260 (12.3%) on colchicine vs 42/263 (16.0%) on usual care, HR 0.77 (95% CI 0.48-1.22). Small-vessel occlusion: 39/419 (9.3%) vs 47/435 (10.8%). Useful as supporting detail alongside the atherosclerosis-stratified analysis, but adds little independent evidence given the null interaction and wide confidence intervals.
updates.citation: Maes L, Walsh C, Weimar C, Purroy F, Price C, Clarke B, et al. Effect of colchicine for secondary prevention according to stroke subtype: a secondary analysis of the CONVINCE randomized trial. Int J Stroke. 2026;21(7):1009-1018. doi:10.1177/17474930251406818.

updates.topic: Moderate-intensity statin plus ezetimibe versus high-intensity statin in acute cerebrovascular disease (MESIA)
updates.whatIsNew: Small single-centre randomised trial (Sun Yat-Sen University), 150 patients with acute ischaemic cerebrovascular disease (mild stroke NIHSS<=5 within 1 week, TIA within 1 week, severe cases within 1 month), randomised to moderate-intensity statin plus ezetimibe 10 mg versus high-intensity statin for 3 months. The primary endpoint was a SURROGATE — LDL-C <=1.8 mmol/L or >=50% reduction at 3 months — and favoured the combination (odds ratio 0.273, 95% CI 0.106-0.705 for the comparison as reported, p=0.005). Include only if the monograph wants to argue for upfront statin-plus-ezetimibe as the document's Step 1-2 shortcut; the trial is far too small and too short for clinical outcomes and should not be cited as event-reduction evidence.
updates.citation: Lv X, Liu X, Peng Y, Li W, Wang J, Chen X, et al. Medium-intensity statin with ezetimibe versus high-intensity statin in acute ischemic cerebrovascular disease (MESIA): a randomized clinical trial. J Stroke Cerebrovasc Dis. 2024;33(5):107647. doi:10.1016/j.jstrokecerebrovasdis.2024.107647.
